problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers. Find the smallest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$:
$$
C\left(a^{2} b+b^{2} c+c^{2} a\right)\left(a b^{2}+b c^{2}+c a^{2}\right) \geq(a b+b c+c a)^{3}
$$
solution:
By Hölder's inequality for the triples:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right)=(1,1,1), \quad\left(b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}\right)=\left(\sqrt[3]{a^{2} b}, \sqrt[3]{b^{2} c}, \sqrt[3]{c^{2} a}\right) \\
& \left(c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}\right)=\left(\sqrt[3]{b^{2} a}, \sqrt[3]{c^{2} b}, \sqrt[3]{a^{2} c}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
we obtain the given inequality.

Equality holds when $a = b = c$, in which case both sides of the inequality are equal and $C = 3$ is achieved. This gives the minimum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 3$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} ; b_{1}, b_{2}$, $\ldots, b_{n} ; m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}$ be three sequences of positive real numbers and let $p>1$. Then
$$
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(a_{i}+b_{i}\right)^{p} m_{i}\right)^{\frac{1}{p}} \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{p} m_{i}\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}^{p} m_{i}\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}
$$

Equality occurs if and only if $\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}=\frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}=\cdots=\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}$.

Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} ; b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be positive real numbers and $p, q>1$ be such that $1 / p+1 / q=1$.
Then
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} b_{i} \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{p}\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}^{q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}}
$$

Equality occurs if and only if $\frac{a_{1}^{p}}{b_{1}^{q}}=\frac{a_{2}^{p}}{b_{2}^{q}}=\cdots=\frac{a_{n}^{p}}{b_{n}^{q}}$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be non-negative real numbers such that $a + b + c = 1$. Find the minimal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
7(ab + bc + ca) \leq C + 9abc
$$
solution:
Let $p=a+b+c=1, q=ab+bc+ca, r=abc$.
Then according to $N_{8}: 2p^3 + 9r \geq 7pq$ we have
$$
2 + 9r \geq 7q \text{ i.e. } \quad 2 + 9abc \geq 7(ab + bc + ca)
$$
as required.

Equality holds when two of the variables are zero and the third is one, i.e., $(a, b, c)$ is a permutation of $(1, 0, 0)$. In this case, $ab + bc + ca = 0$ and $abc = 0$, so the inequality becomes $0 \leq 2$, which is tight for $C = 2$. This gives the minimum value of $C$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 2$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $x, y, z \geq 0$, and $p=x+y+z, q=x y+y z+z x, r=x y z$.
Then we have the following inequalities:
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
N_{3}: p q-9 r \geq 0, & N_{9}: p^{4}+3 q^{2} \geq 4 p^{2} q \\
N_{4}: p^{2} \geq 3 q, & N_{10}: 2 p^{3}+9 r^{2} \geq 7 p q r \\
N_{5}: p^{3} \geq 27 r, & N_{11}: p^{2} q+3 p r \geq 4 q^{2} \\
N_{6}: q^{3} \geq 27 r^{2}, & N_{12}: q^{3}+9 r^{2} \geq 4 p q r \\
N_{7}: q^{2} \geq 3 p r, & N_{13}: p q^{2} \geq 2 p^{2} r+3 q r \\
N_{8}: 2 p^{3}+9 r \geq 7 p q, &
\end{array}
$$

problem:
Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers. Find the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$:
$$
\frac{x+y}{z}+\frac{y+z}{x}+\frac{z+x}{y} \geq C\left(\frac{z}{x+y}+\frac{x}{y+z}+\frac{y}{z+x}\right)
$$
solution:
Consider the function $f(x)=x+\frac{1}{x}$.
Since $f^{\prime}(x)=1-\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x)=\frac{2}{x^{3}}>0$ for any $x>0$ it follows that $f$ is convex on $\mathbb{R}^{+}$.

Now by Popoviciu's inequality we can easily obtain the required inequality.

Equality holds when $x = y = z$, in which case both sides of the inequality are equal and $C$ attains its maximum value. Thus, $C = 4$ is the largest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 4$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $f:[a, b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a convex function on the interval $[a, b]$. Then for any $x, y, z \in[a, b]$ we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
& f\left(\frac{x+y+z}{3}\right)+\frac{f(x)+f(y)+f(z)}{3} \\
& \quad \geq \frac{2}{3}\left(f\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)+f\left(\frac{y+z}{2}\right)+f\left(\frac{z+x}{2}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $a + b + c = 1$. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
10\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)-9\left(a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{5}\right) \geq C
$$
solution:
Denote $L=10\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)-9\left(a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{5}\right)$.
Let $x=a+b+c=1, y=a b+b c+c a, z=a b c$.
Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
10\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right) & =10\left((a+b+c)^{3}-3(a+b+c)(a b+b c+c a)+3 a b c\right) \\
& =10-30 y+30 z
\end{aligned}
$$
and
$$
\begin{aligned}
9\left(a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{5}\right) & =9\left(x^{5}-5 x^{3} y+5 x y^{2}+5 x^{2} z-5 y z\right) \\
& =9\left(1-5 y+5 y^{2}+5 z-5 y z\right) \\
& =9-45 y+45 y^{2}+45 z-45 y z
\end{aligned}
$$

We have
$$
L \geq 1 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad 10-30 y+30 z-9+45 y-45 y^{2}-45 z+45 y z \geq 1
$$
i.e.
$$
1+15 y-15 z-45 y^{2}+45 y z \geq 1
$$
i.e.
$$
\begin{equation*}
y-z-3 y(y-z) \geq 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad(1-3 y)(y-z) \geq 0 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

Furthermore,
$$
y=a b+b c+c a \leq \frac{(a+b+c)^{2}}{3}=\frac{1}{3}, \quad \text { i.e. } \quad 1-3 y \geq 0
$$
and
$$
y=a b+b c+c a \geq 3 \sqrt[3]{a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}}=3 \sqrt[3]{z^{2}}>z
$$

The last inequality is true since
$$
z=a b c \leq\left(\frac{a+b+c}{3}\right)^{3}=1<27
$$

From the previous two inequalities we get inequality (1), as desired.

Equality holds when $a = b = c = \frac{1}{3}$, since then $y = 3 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{3}$ and $z = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{27}$, and the original expression evaluates to $L = 1$. This gives the minimum value of $L$, so $C = 1$ is the largest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

theorems.Theorem:
If $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ are nonnegative real numbers, then

$$
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} \geq\left(a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n}}
$$

with equality if and only if $a_{1}=a_{2}=\ldots=a_{n}$. This inequality is a special case of the Power Mean Inequality.

problem:
Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $a + b + c = 1$. Find the minimal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
7(a b + b c + c a) \leq 9 a b c + C
$$
solution:
$$
f(a, b, c)=7(a b+b c+c a)-9 a b c-2, \quad g(a, b, c)=a+b+c-1
$$
and
$$
L=f-\lambda g=7(a b+b c+c a)-9 a b c-2-\lambda(a+b+c-1)
$$

We have
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a}=7(b+c)-9 b c-\lambda=0 \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \lambda=7(b+c)-9 b c \\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=7(c+a)-9 c a-\lambda=0 \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \lambda=7(c+a)-9 c a \\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}=7(a+b)-9 a b-\lambda=0 \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \lambda=7(a+b)-9 a b
\end{array}
$$

So
$$
\begin{equation*}
7(b+c)-9 b c=\lambda=7(c+a)-9 c a \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad(b-a)(7-9 c)=0 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

In the same way we obtain
$$
\begin{equation*}
(c-b)(7-9 a)=0 \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$
and
$$
\begin{equation*}
(a-c)(7-9 b)=0 \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

Let us consider the identity (1).
If $a=b$ then if $b=c$ we get $a=b=c=1 / 3$, and then
$$
f(a, b, c)=7(a b+b c+c a)-9 a b c-2=\frac{21}{9}-\frac{9}{27}-2=0
$$

If $a=b$ and $b \neq c$ then by (2) we must have $a=\frac{7}{9}=b$ and then $a+b=\frac{14}{9}>1$, a contradiction, since $a+b<a+b+c=1$.

If $7-9 c=0$ then we can't have $7-9 a=0$ or $7-9 b=0$ for the same reasons as before, so according to (2) and (3) we must have $b=c$ and $a=c$, i.e. $a=b=c=7 / 9$, which is impossible.

Therefore $\min L=0$, i.e. $7(a b+b c+c a) \leq 9 a b c+2$.

Equality holds when $a = b = c = \frac{1}{3}$, since then $a + b + c = 1$ and $7(a b + b c + c a) - 9 a b c = 2$. This gives the maximum value of $7(a b + b c + c a) - 9 a b c$ for the given constraint, so the minimal constant $C$ is $2$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 2$.

theorems.Theorem: Let $f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{m}\right)$ be a continuous and differentiable function on $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m}$, and let $g_{i}\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{m}\right)$ $=0, i=1,2, \ldots, k$, where $(k<m)$ are the conditions that must be satisfied. Then the maximum or minimum values of $f$ with the conditions $g_{i}\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots\right.$, $\left.x_{m}\right)=0, i=1,2, \ldots, k$, occur at the bounds of the interval $I$ or occur at the points at which the partial derivatives (according to the variables $\left.x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{m}\right)$ of the function $L=f-\sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_{i} g_{i}$, are all zero.

problem:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be the lengths of the sides of a given $n$-gon $(n \geq 3)$ and let $s = a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n}$. Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$:

$$
\frac{a_{1}}{s-2a_{1}} + \frac{a_{2}}{s-2a_{2}} + \cdots + \frac{a_{n}}{s-2a_{n}} \geq C.
$$
solution:
Without loss of generality we may assume that $a_{1} \geq a_{2} \geq \cdots \geq a_{n}$. Then clearly $0<s-2 a_{1} \leq s-2 a_{2} \leq \cdots \leq s-2 a_{n}$.

We obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a_{1}}{s-2 a_{1}}+\frac{a_{2}}{s-2 a_{2}}+\cdots+\frac{a_{n}}{s-2 a_{n}} & =\frac{a_{1} \cdot 1}{s-2 a_{1}}+\frac{a_{2} \cdot 1}{s-2 a_{2}}+\cdots+\frac{a_{n} \cdot 1}{s-2 a_{n}} \\
& \geq \frac{\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right) n}{n s-2\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)} \\
& =\frac{n s}{s(n-2)}=\frac{n}{n-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Equality holds when all $a_i$ are equal, i.e., $a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_n$, so $s = n a_1$ and each term is $\frac{a_1}{n a_1 - 2 a_1} = \frac{1}{n-2}$, summing to $\frac{n}{n-2}$. This gives the minimum value of the sum, so $C = \frac{n}{n-2}$ is maximal.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{n}{n-2}$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $a_{1} \leq a_{2} \leq \cdots \leq a_{n}$; $b_{1} \leq b_{2} \leq \cdots \leq b_{n}$ be real numbers and let $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}$ be non-negative real numbers such that $m_{1}+m_{2}+\cdots+m_{n}=1$.
Then
$$
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} m_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i} m_{i}\right) \leq \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} b_{i} m_{i}
$$

Equality occurs iff $a_{1}=a_{2}=\cdots=a_{n}$ or $b_{1}=b_{2}=\cdots=b_{n}$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be the lengths of the sides of a given triangle. Find the maximal constant $C_1$ and the minimal constant $C_2$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$:
$$
C_1 \leq \frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{c+a}+\frac{c}{a+b} \leq C_2
$$
solution:
Let's prove the right-hand inequality.
Since $a+b>c$ we have $2(a+b)>a+b+c$, i.e. $a+b>s$.
Similarly we get $b+c>s$ and $a+c>s$.
Therefore
$$
\frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{a+c}+\frac{c}{b+a}<\frac{a}{s}+\frac{b}{s}+\frac{c}{s}=2
$$

Let's consider the left-hand inequality.
If we denote $b+c=x, a+c=y, a+b=z$ then we have
$$
a=\frac{z+y-x}{2}, \quad b=\frac{z+x-y}{2}, \quad c=\frac{x+y-z}{2} .
$$

Hence
$$
\frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{a+c}+\frac{c}{b+a}=\frac{z+y-x}{2 x}+\frac{z+x-y}{2 y}+\frac{x+y-z}{2 z}
$$
i.e.
$\frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{a+c}+\frac{c}{b+a}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{z}{x}+\frac{y}{x}+\frac{z}{y}+\frac{x}{y}+\frac{x}{z}+\frac{y}{x}-3\right) \geq \frac{1}{2}(2+2+2-3)=\frac{3}{2}$,
as required.

Equality in the left-hand inequality holds when the triangle is equilateral, i.e., $a = b = c$, giving $\frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{c+a}+\frac{c}{a+b} = \frac{3}{2}$. Equality in the right-hand inequality is approached as one side tends to zero (degenerate triangle), so the maximum value is $2$ but never actually attained for a non-degenerate triangle. Thus, $C_1 = \frac{3}{2}$ is the minimum and $C_2 = 2$ is the maximum value of the expression.

Therefore, the answer is $C_1 = \frac{3}{2}, \quad C_2 = 2$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$, and let us denote
$$
\begin{aligned}
Q M & =\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{3}}, \quad A M=\frac{a+b+c}{3}, \quad G M=\sqrt[3]{a b c} \text { and } \\
H M & =\frac{3}{\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then
$$
Q M \geq A M \geq G M \geq H M
$$

Equalities occur if and only if $a=b=c$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$:
$$
3\left(a^{2}-a b+b^{2}\right)\left(b^{2}-b c+c^{2}\right)\left(c^{2}-c a+a^{2}\right) \geq C(a^{3} b^{3}+b^{3} c^{3}+c^{3} a^{3})
$$
solution:
It is enough to consider the case when $a, b, c \geq 0$.
We have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(a^{2}-a b+b^{2}\right)\left(b^{2}-b c+c^{2}\right)\left(c^{2}-c a+a^{2}\right)= & \sum_{\mathrm{sym}} a^{4} b^{2}-\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} a^{3} b^{3}-\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} a^{4} b c \\
& +a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The given inequality is equivalent to
$$
3\sum_{\text {sym }} a^{4} b^{2}-4 \sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} a^{3} b^{3}-3 \sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} a^{4} b c+3 a^{2} b^{2} c^{2} \geq 0
$$
which is equivalent to
$$
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\left(2 c^{4}+3 a^{2} b^{2}-a b c(a+b+c)\right)(a-b)^{2} \geq 0 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

Assume $a \geq b \geq c$ and denote
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S_{a}=2 a^{4}+3 b^{2} c^{2}-a b c(a+b+c) \\
& S_{b}=2 b^{4}+3 a^{2} c^{2}-a b c(a+b+c)
\end{aligned}
$$
and
$$
S_{c}=2 c^{4}+3 a^{2} b^{2}-a b c(a+b+c)
$$

We have
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S_{a}=2 a^{4}+3 b^{2} c^{2}-a b c(a+b+c) \geq a^{4}+2 a^{2} b c-a b c(a+b+c) \geq 0 \\
& S_{c}=2 c^{4}+3 a^{2} b^{2}-a b c(a+b+c) \geq 3 a^{2} b^{2}-a b c(a+b+c) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{a}+2 S_{b} & =2 a^{4}+3 b^{2} c^{2}+4 b^{4}+6 a^{2} c^{2}-3 a b c(a+b+c) \\
& \geq a^{4}+2 a^{2} b c+8 b^{2} c a-3 a b c(a+b+c) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
and
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{c}+2 S_{b} & =2 c^{4}+3 a^{2} b^{2}+4 b^{4}+6 a^{2} c^{2}-3 a b c(a+b+c) \\
& \geq\left(3 a^{2} b^{2}+3 a^{2} c^{2}\right)+3 a^{2} c^{2}-3 a b c(a+b+c) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
(Since the given inequality is cyclic if we assume that $a \leq b \leq c$ similarly we can show that $S_{a}, S_{c}, S_{a}+2 S_{b}, S_{c}+2 S_{b} \geq 0$.)

According to the SOS theorem we obtain that inequality (1) holds, as required.

Equality holds when $a = b = c$, in which case both sides of the inequality are equal. This gives the minimum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds, so the largest constant is $C = 1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Given a function $f$ of $n$ variables, define the cyclic sum of variables $\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ as

$$
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{c y c} f\left(x_{1}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)=f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)+f\left(x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{n}, x_{1}\right) \\
+\ldots+f\left(a_{n}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n-1}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

problem:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$. Find the smallest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$:
$$
a^{2}+b^{2}+C > a \sqrt{b^{2}+1}+b \sqrt{a^{2}+1}
$$
solution:
From the obvious inequality
$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(a-\sqrt{b^{2}+1}\right)^{2}+\left(b-\sqrt{a^{2}+1}\right)^{2} \geq 0 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$
we get the desired result.
Equality occurs if and only if
$$
a=\sqrt{b^{2}+1} \quad \text { and } \quad b=\sqrt{a^{2}+1}, \quad \text { i.e. } \quad a^{2}=b^{2}+1 \quad \text { and } \quad b^{2}=a^{2}+1
$$
which is impossible, so in (1) we have strictly inequality.

The minimum value of $C$ is achieved in the limit as $a$ and $b$ approach $0$, where the inequality becomes $C > 1$. Thus, the smallest constant $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = 1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Let $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 2$. Find the smallest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x, y, z$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
x + y + z \leq C + x y z
$$
solution:
Let $x=a \sqrt{2}, y=b \sqrt{2}, z=c \sqrt{2}$. Then $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=1$ and the given inequality becomes $a+b+c-2 a b c \leq \sqrt{2}$, which is true.

Equality holds when two of $a, b, c$ are zero and the third is $1$ (or permutations), which corresponds to $x = \sqrt{2}, y = 0, z = 0$ (and permutations). In this case, $x + y + z = \sqrt{2}$ and $x y z = 0$, so $C = 2$ is the smallest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 2$.

The given inequality becomes
$$
x(1-y z)+y+z \leq 2
$$

Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
& (x(1-y z)+(y+z) \cdot 1)^{2} \leq\left(x^{2}+(y+z)^{2}\right)\left((1-y z)^{2}+1^{2}\right) \\
& \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad(x+y+z-x y z)^{2} \leq\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+2 y z\right)\left(2-2 y z+y^{2} z^{2}\right) \\
& \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad(x+y+z-x y z)^{2} \leq 2(1+y z)\left(2-2 y z+y^{2} z^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

So it suffices to show that
$$
2(1+y z)\left(2-2 y z+y^{2} z^{2}\right) \leq 4
$$
i.e.
$$
(1+y z)\left(2-2 y z+y^{2} z^{2}\right) \leq 2 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad y^{3} z^{3} \leq y^{2} z^{2}
$$
i.e.
$$
y z \leq 1
$$

The last inequality is true since $2 y z \leq y^{2}+z^{2} \leq x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=2$.

Equality holds when $y = z = 1$ and $x = 0$, or any permutation thereof, since then $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 + 0^2 = 2$ and $x + y + z = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2$, $x y z = 0$, so $x + y + z = 2 = 2 + 0$. This gives the minimum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds, so $C = 2$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 2$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}$, $\ldots, b_{n}$ be real numbers. Then we have
$$
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}^{2}\right) \geq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} b_{i}\right)^{2}
$$
i.e.
$$
\left(a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\cdots+a_{n}^{2}\right)\left(b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}+\cdots+b_{n}^{2}\right) \geq\left(a_{1} b_{1}+a_{2} b_{2}+\cdots+a_{n} b_{n}\right)^{2}
$$

Equality occurs if and only if the sequences $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\right)$ and $\left(b_{1}, b_{2}\right.$, $\ldots, b_{n}$ ) are proportional, i.e. $\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}=\frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}=\cdots=\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}$.

problem:
Let $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $x y z=1$. Find the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x, y, z$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+x y+y z+z x}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z}} \geq C
$$
solution:
We have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+x y+y z+z x}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z}} & =\frac{x^{2}+y z+y^{2}+z x+z^{2}+x y}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z}} \\
& \geq \frac{2 \sqrt{x^{2} y z}+2 \sqrt{x y^{2} z}+2 \sqrt{x y z^{2}}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z}} \\
& =\frac{2(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z})}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z}}=2
\end{aligned}
$$

Equality holds if and only if $x = y = z = 1$, which gives the minimum value of the expression. Thus, the maximal constant $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = 2$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 2$.

problem:
Let $a_{1} \leq a_{2} \leq \cdots \leq a_{n}$ and $b_{1} \leq b_{2} \leq \cdots \leq b_{n}$ be two sequences of real numbers. Determine the minimal constant $C$ such that for any permutation $\left(c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{n}\right)$ of $\left(b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}\right)$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\left(a_{1}-b_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(a_{2}-b_{2}\right)^{2}+\cdots+\left(a_{n}-b_{n}\right)^{2} \leq C \left(a_{1}-b_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(a_{2}-b_{2}\right)^{2}+\cdots+\left(a_{n}-b_{n}\right)^{2}.
$$
solution:
Note that $b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}+\\cdots+b_{n}^{2}=c_{1}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}+\\cdots+c_{n}^{2}$.

$$
a_{1} c_{1}+a_{2} c_{2}+\cdots+a_{n} c_{n} \leq a_{1} b_{1}+a_{2} b_{2}+\cdots+a_{n} b_{n}

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$. Find the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$:
$$
(a+b)^{4}+(b+c)^{4}+(c+a)^{4} \geq C\left(a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}\right)
$$
solution:
Since
$$
\begin{aligned}
&(a+b)^{4}+(b+c)^{4}+(c+a)^{4} \\
& \quad= 2\left(a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}\right)+4\left(a^{3} b+b^{3} a+b^{3} c+c^{3} b+c^{3} a+a^{3} c\right) \\
&+6\left(a^{2} b^{2}+b^{2} c^{2}+c^{2} a^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
the given inequality becomes
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 5\left(a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}\right)+14\left(a^{3} b+b^{3} a+b^{3} c+c^{3} b+c^{3} a+a^{3} c\right) \\
& \quad+21\left(a^{2} b^{2}+b^{2} c^{2}+c^{2} a^{2}\right) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

After setting $a+b+c=p, ab+bc+ca=\frac{p^{2}-q^{2}}{3}, r=abc$, due to $5^{\circ}, 6^{\circ}$ and $7^{\circ}$ we deduce that the previous inequality is equivalent to
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 5\left(\frac{-p^{4}+8 p^{2} q^{2}+2 q^{4}}{9}+4 p r\right)+14\left(\frac{\left(p^{2}+2 q^{2}\right)\left(p^{2}-q^{2}\right)}{9}-p r\right) \\
& \quad+21\left(\frac{\left(p^{2}-q^{2}\right)^{2}}{9}-2 p r\right) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
i.e.
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 5\left(-p^{4}+8 p^{2} q^{2}+2 q^{4}+36 p r\right)+14\left(\left(p^{2}+2 q^{2}\right)\left(p^{2}-q^{2}\right)-9 p r\right) \\
& \quad+21\left(\left(p^{2}-q^{2}\right)^{2}-18 p r\right) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

If $p=0$ then $10 q^{4}-28 q^{4}+21 q^{4} \geq 0$, i.e. $3 q^{4} \geq 0$, which is obvious.
Let $p \neq 0$.
Without loss of generality we may assume that $p=1$.
So we need to prove that
$5\left(-1+8 q^{2}+2 q^{4}+36 r\right)+14\left(\left(1+2 q^{2}\right)\left(1-q^{2}\right)-9 r\right)+21\left(\left(1-q^{2}\right)^{2}-18 r\right) \geq 0$, i.e.
$$
3 q^{4}+4 q^{2}+10-108 r \geq 0
$$

We obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
3 q^{4}+4 q^{2}+10-108 r & \geq 3 q^{4}+4 q^{2}+10-108 \frac{(1-q)^{2}(1+2 q)}{27} \\
& =3 q^{4}+4 q^{2}+10-4(1-q)^{2}(1+2 q) \\
& =q^{2}(q-4)^{2}+2 q^{4}+6 \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
which clearly holds.
Equality occurs if and only if $a=b=c=0$.

Equality in the above occurs only when $a = b = c = 0$, in which case both sides of the original inequality are zero. This gives the maximum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{4}{7}$.

problem:
If $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z}=1$, then determine the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x, y, z$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
(1-x)^{2}(1-y)^{2}(1-z)^{2} \geq C \cdot x y z (x+y)(y+z)(z+x)
$$
solution:
We put $a=\sqrt{x}, b=\sqrt{y}$ and $c=\sqrt{z}$. Then $1-x=1-a^{2}=(a+b+c)^{2}-a^{2}=(b+c)(2 a+b+c)$. Now we have to prove that $((a+b)(b+c)(c+a)(2 a+b+c)(a+2 b+c)(a+b+2 c))^{2} \geq 2^{15} a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)\left(c^{2}+a^{2}\right)$. But this inequality is true as it follows from the following true inequalities $a b\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right) \leq \frac{(a+b)^{4}}{8}$ (this being equivalent to $(a-b)^{4} \geq 0$) and $(2 a+b+c)(a+2 b+c)(a+b+2 c) \geq 8(b+c)(c+a)(a+b)$.

Equality holds when $a = b = c = \frac{1}{3}$, that is, $x = y = z = \frac{1}{9}$. In this case, both sides of the inequality are equal, so the maximum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = 2^{15}$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 2^{15}$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c, x, y, z > 0$. Find the smallest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c, x, y, z$:
$$
\frac{a x}{a+x}+\frac{b y}{b+y}+\frac{c z}{c+z} \leq C \cdot \frac{(a+b+c)(x+y+z)}{a+b+c+x+y+z}
$$
solution:
We'll use the following lemma.
For every $p, q, \alpha, \beta>0$ we have
$$
\frac{p q}{p+q} \leq \frac{\alpha^{2} p+\beta^{2} q}{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}}
$$

Proof The given inequality is equivalent to $(\alpha p-\beta q)^{2} \geq 0$.

Now let $\alpha=x+y+z, \beta=a+b+c$, and applying Lemma 21.1, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{a x}{a+x} \leq \frac{(x+y+z)^{2} a+(a+b+c)^{2} x}{(x+y+z+a+b+c)^{2}} \\
& \frac{b y}{b+y} \leq \frac{(x+y+z)^{2} b+(a+b+c)^{2} y}{(x+y+z+a+b+c)^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$
and
$$
\frac{c z}{c+z} \leq \frac{(x+y+z)^{2} c+(a+b+c)^{2} z}{(x+y+z+a+b+c)^{2}}
$$

Adding these inequalities we get the required result.

Equality holds when $a : b : c = x : y : z$, that is, when $a = x$, $b = y$, $c = z$. In this case, both sides of the inequality are equal, and the minimum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = 1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 3$. Determine the minimal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$:
$$
\sqrt[3]{a^2 + bc} + \sqrt[3]{b^2 + ca} + \sqrt[3]{c^2 + ab} \leq C.
$$
solution:
Since we have a symmetrical expression we estimate that the maximum value will occur at the point of incidence $a=b=c=1$. Then we have $a^{2}+b c=2$.

By the inequality $A M \geq G M$ we get
$$
\sqrt[3]{a^{2}+b c}=\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{4}} \cdot \sqrt[3]{\left(a^{2}+b c\right) \cdot 2 \cdot 2} \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{4}}\left(\frac{a^{2}+b c+4}{3}\right)
$$

Similarly we obtain
$$
\sqrt[3]{b^{2}+c a} \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{4}}\left(\frac{b^{2}+c a+4}{3}\right) \quad \text { and } \quad \sqrt[3]{c^{2}+a b} \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{4}}\left(\frac{c^{2}+a b+4}{3}\right)
$$

Adding the last three inequalities gives us
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt[3]{a^{2}+b c}+\sqrt[3]{b^{2}+c a}+\sqrt[3]{c^{2}+a b} & \leq \frac{1}{3 \sqrt[3]{4}}\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+a b+b c+c a+12\right) \\
& \leq \frac{1}{3 \sqrt[3]{4}}\left(2\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)+12\right)=\frac{18}{3 \sqrt[3]{4}}=3 \sqrt[3]{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Equality occurs if and only if $a = b = c = 1$, which satisfies $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 3$ and gives $\sqrt[3]{a^2 + bc} = \sqrt[3]{2}$ for each term, so the sum is $3 \sqrt[3]{2}$. Thus, this gives the maximum value of the expression, so $C = 3 \sqrt[3]{2}$ is minimal such that the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 3 \sqrt[3]{2}$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c > 0$ be real numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 12$. Find the minimal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c > 0$:
$$
a \sqrt[3]{b^2 + c^2} + b \sqrt[3]{c^2 + a^2} + c \sqrt[3]{a^2 + b^2} \leq C.
$$
solution:
Since $A$ is a symmetrical expression with respect to $a, b$ and $c, \max A$ occurs when $a=b=c>0$, i.e. $a=b=c=2$.

Hence
$$
2 a^{2}=2 b^{2}=2 c^{2}=8
$$
and
$$
b^{2}+c^{2}=c^{2}+a^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}=8
$$

By $A M \geq G M$ we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
a \sqrt[3]{b^{2}+c^{2}} & =\sqrt[3]{a^{3}\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)}=\sqrt[6]{a^{6}\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt[6]{\left(2 a^{2}\right)^{3} \cdot\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)^{2} \cdot 8} \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \sqrt[6]{8\left(2 a^{2}\right)\left(2 a^{2}\right)\left(2 a^{2}\right)\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)} \\
& \leq \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{8+6 a^{2}+2\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)}{6}=\frac{4+3 a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly
$$
b \sqrt[3]{c^{2}+a^{2}} \leq \frac{4+a^{2}+3 b^{2}+c^{2}}{6} \quad \text { and } \quad c \sqrt[3]{a^{2}+b^{2}} \leq \frac{4+a^{2}+b^{2}+3 c^{2}}{6}
$$

After adding the last three inequalities we get
$$
A \leq \frac{12+5\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)}{6}=\frac{12+5 \cdot 12}{6}=12
$$
with equality if and only if $a=b=c=2$.

Equality holds when $a = b = c = 2$, since then $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 12$ and each term is maximized, so the maximum value of $A$ is $12$. Thus, $C = 12$ is the minimal constant such that the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 12$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $a b c = 1$. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{6}{a+b+c} \geq C
$$
solution:
Without loss of generality we may assume that $a \geq b \geq c$.
Let $f(a, b, c)=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{6}{a+b+c}$.
We'll prove that
$$
f(a, b, c) \geq f(a, \sqrt{b c}, \sqrt{b c})
$$

We have
$$
\begin{align*}
f(a, b, c) & \geq f(a, \sqrt{b c}, \sqrt{b c}) \\
\Leftrightarrow & \quad \frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}+\frac{6}{a+b+c} \geq \frac{2}{\sqrt{b c}}+\frac{6}{a+2 \sqrt{b c}} \\
\Leftrightarrow & c(a+b+c)(a+2 \sqrt{b c})+b(a+b+c)(a+2 \sqrt{b c})+6 b c(a+2 \sqrt{b c}) \\
& \geq 2 \sqrt{b c}(a+b+c)(a+2 \sqrt{b c})+6 b c(a+b+c) \\
\Leftrightarrow & (\sqrt{b}-\sqrt{c})^{2}((a+b+c)(a+2 \sqrt{b c})-6 b c) \geq 0 \tag{1}
\end{align*}
$$

Since $a \geq b \geq c$ we have $a \geq \frac{b+c}{2} \geq \sqrt{b c}$.
Thus
$$
(a+b+c)(a+2 \sqrt{b c}) \geq(\sqrt{b c}+2 \sqrt{b c})(\sqrt{b c}+2 \sqrt{b c})=9 b c \geq 6 b c
$$

So due to (1) and the last inequality we have
$$
f(a, b, c) \geq f(a, \sqrt{b c}, \sqrt{b c})
$$

According to the SMV theorem we need to prove that $f(a, t, t) \geq 5$, with $a t^{2}=1$.
We have
$$
f(a, t, t) \geq 5 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \frac{1}{a}+\frac{2}{t}+\frac{6}{a+2 t} \geq 5
$$
which is equivalent to
$$
(t-1)^{2}\left(2 t^{4}+4 t^{3}-4 t^{2}-t+2\right) \geq 0
$$
which is true since $2 t^{4}+4 t^{3}-4 t^{2}-t+2>0$ for $t>0$.

Equality holds when $a = b = c = 1$, since $abc = 1$ and $a + b + c = 3$, so $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} + \frac{6}{a + b + c} = 3 + 2 = 5$. This gives the minimum value of $f(a, b, c)$, so the largest constant $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = 5$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 5$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $abc = 1$. Determine the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$:

\frac{a^{3} c}{(b+c)(c+a)}+\frac{b^{3} a}{(c+a)(a+b)}+\frac{c^{3} b}{(a+b)(b+c)} \geq C.
$$
solution:
Clearing denominators gives us
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 4\left(a^{4} c+b^{4} a+c^{4} a+a^{3} c b+b^{3} a c+c^{3} b a\right) \\
& \quad \geq 3\left(a^{2} b+a^{2} c+b^{2} a+b^{2} c+c^{2} a+c^{2} b+2 a b c\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
i.e.
$4\left(a^{4} c+b^{4} a+c^{4} a+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right) \geq 3\left(a^{2} b+a^{2} c+b^{2} a+b^{2} c+c^{2} a+c^{2} b+2\right)$.
By $A M \geq G M$ and $a b c=1$ we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 4\left(a^{4} c+b^{4} a+c^{4} a+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right) \\
& =\left(a^{4} c+a^{2}+b^{4} a\right)+\left(b^{4} a+b^{2}+c^{4} b\right)+\left(c^{4} b+c^{2}+a^{4} c\right)+\left(a^{4} c+a^{2}+c^{2}\right) \\
& +\left(b^{4} a+b^{2}+a^{2}\right)+\left(c^{4} b+c^{2}+b^{2}\right)+\left(a^{4} c+b^{4} a+c^{4} b\right)+\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right) \\
& \geq 3 \sqrt[3]{a^{6} b^{3}}+3 \sqrt[3]{b^{6} c^{3}}+3 \sqrt[3]{c^{6} a^{3}}+3 \sqrt[3]{a^{6} c^{3}}+3 \sqrt[3]{c^{6} b^{3}}+3 \sqrt[3]{a^{5} b^{5} c^{5}} \\
& +3 \sqrt[3]{a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}} \\
& =3\left(a^{2} b+a^{2} c+b^{2} a+b^{2} c+c^{2} a+c^{2} b+2\right),
\end{aligned}
$$
and we are done.

Equality holds when $a = b = c = 1$, since $abc = 1$ and all terms become equal, achieving the minimum value of the expression. Thus, $C = \frac{3}{4}$ is the largest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{3}{4}$.

The given inequality becomes
$$
3\left(p^{2}-2 q\right)+r \geq 10, \quad \text { with constraint } q+r=4
$$

So it is enough to show that
$$
\begin{equation*}
3 p^{2}-6 q+4-q \geq 10, \quad \text { i.e. } \quad 3 p^{2}-7 q-6 \geq 0 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

Applying $N_{1}: p^{3}-4 p q+9 r \geq 0$ (Chap. 14), and since $q+r=4$ we deuce
$$
p^{3}-4 p q+9(4-q) \geq 0, \quad \text { i.e. } \quad q \leq \frac{p^{3}+36}{4 p+9}
$$

So
$$
\begin{equation*}
3 p^{2}-7 q-6 \geq 3 p^{2}-7 \frac{p^{3}+36}{4 p+9}-6=\frac{(p-3)\left(5 p^{2}+42 p+102\right)}{4 p+9} \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

Applying $A M \geq G M$ we obtain
$$
\begin{align*}
4 & =x y+y z+z x+x y z \geq 4 \sqrt[4]{(x y z)^{3}} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \quad 1 \geq x y z \tag{3}
\end{align*}
$$

Also $(x+y+z)^{2} \geq 3(x y+y z+z x)$, so we deduce
$$
p=x+y+z \geq \sqrt{3(4-x y z)} \stackrel{(3)}{\geq} \sqrt{3(4-1)}=3 .
$$

Finally by using (2) we obtain that $3 p^{2}-7 q-6 \geq 0$, i.e. inequality (1) holds.

Equality holds when $x = y = z = 1$, since then $xy + yz + zx + xyz = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4$ and $3(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) + xyz = 3(1 + 1 + 1) + 1 = 10$. This gives the minimum value of the expression, so $C = 10$ is the largest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 10$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be positive real numbers. The numbers
$$
\begin{aligned}
& Q M=\sqrt{\frac{a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\cdots+a_{n}^{2}}{n}}, \quad A M=\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}}{n} \\
& G M=\sqrt[n]{a_{1} a_{2} \cdots a_{n}} \quad \text { and } \quad H M=\frac{n}{\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\frac{1}{a_{2}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}}
\end{aligned}
$$
are called the quadratic, arithmetic, geometric and harmonic mean for the numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$, respectively, and we have
$$
Q M \geq A M \geq G M \geq H M
$$

Equalities occur if and only if $a_{1}=a_{2}=\cdots=a_{n}$.

problem:
Let $x \geq 3$ be a real number. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x \geq 3$:
$$
x + \frac{1}{x} \geq C
$$
solution:
In this case we cannot directly use the inequality $A M \geq G M$ since the point $x=1$ doesn't belongs to the domain $[3,+\infty)$.

We can easily show that the function $f(x)=x+\frac{1}{x}$ is an increasing function on $[3,+\infty)$, so it follows that $\min \left\{x+\frac{1}{x}\right\}=3+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{10}{3}$.

Now we will show how we can use $A M \geq G M$.
Since we have equality in $A M \geq G M$ if and only if all variables are equal, we deduce that we cannot use this inequality for the numbers $x$ and $\frac{1}{x}$ at the point of incidence $x=3$ since $3 \neq \frac{1}{3}$.

Assume that $A M \geq G M$ is used for the couple $\left(\frac{x}{\alpha}, \frac{1}{x}\right)$ such that at the point of incidence $x=3$, equality occurs, i.e. $\frac{x}{\alpha}=\frac{1}{x}$.

So it follows that $\alpha=x^{2}=3^{2}=9$.
According to this we transform $x+\frac{1}{x}$ as follows
$$
A=x+\frac{1}{x}=\frac{x}{9}+\frac{1}{x}+\frac{8}{9} x \geq 2 \sqrt{\frac{x}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{x}}+\frac{8}{9} x=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{8}{9} \cdot 3=\frac{10}{3}
$$

Equality in the above occurs when $x = 3$, since $f(x)$ is increasing for $x \geq 3$ and attains its minimum at $x = 3$. Thus, the minimum value of $x + \frac{1}{x}$ for $x \geq 3$ is $3 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{10}{3}$, so this gives the minimum value of $C$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 3 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{10}{3}$.

problem:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers. Find the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$:
$$
a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\cdots+a_{n}^{2} \geq C\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)
$$
solution:
Without loss of generality, we may assume that $a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{n}$ and hence $a_{i} \geq i$ for all $i$. Thus, we may take $b_{i}=a_{i}-i \geq 0$ and the inequality becomes

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}^{2}+2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} i b_{i}+\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6} \geq \frac{2 n+1}{3} \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}+\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}
$$

Now, using the fact that $a_{i+1}>a_{i}$ we infer that $b_{1} \leq b_{2} \leq \cdots \leq b_{n}$ and from Chebyshev's Inequality we deduce that

$$
2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} i b_{i} \geq(n+1) \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i} \geq \frac{2 n+1}{3} \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}
$$

and the conclusion is immediate. Also, from the above relations we can see immediately that we have equality if and only if $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ is a permutation of the numbers $1,2, \ldots, n$.

Equality holds when $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are exactly $1, 2, \ldots, n$ in some order, i.e., when $b_i = 0$ for all $i$. In this case, the minimum value of $C$ is achieved, so $C = \frac{2n+1}{3}$ is the maximal constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{2n+1}{3}$.

problem:
Let $x, y, z$ be distinct non-negative real numbers. Find the largest positive constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all distinct non-negative real $x, y, z$:
$$
\frac{1}{(x-y)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(y-z)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(z-x)^{2}} \geq \frac{C}{x y+y z+z x}
$$
solution:
If $a, b>0$, then $\frac{1}{(a-b)^{2}}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}} \geq \frac{4}{a b}$.
The last inequality is true since
$$
\frac{1}{(a-b)^{2}}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}-\frac{4}{a b}=\frac{\left(a^{2}+b^{2}-3 a b\right)^{2}}{a^{2} b^{2}(a-b)^{2}}
$$

Without loss of generality we may assume that $z=\min \{x, y, z\}$.
By the previous inequality for $a=x-z$ and $b=y-z$ we get
$$
\frac{1}{(x-y)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(y-z)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(z-x)^{2}} \geq \frac{4}{(x-z)(y-z)}
$$

So it suffices to show that
$$
\frac{4}{(x-z)(y-z)} \geq \frac{4}{x y+y z+z x}
$$
i.e.
$$
x y+y z+z x \geq(x-z)(y-z)
$$
i.e.
$$
2 z(y+x) \geq z^{2}
$$
which is true since $z=\min \{x, y, z\}$.

Equality in the key inequality holds when two of the variables are equal and the third is zero, for example, $x = y > 0$, $z = 0$. In this case, the minimum value of $C$ is achieved, so $C = 4$ is the largest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 4$.

problem:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{3}=3$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{5}=5$. Determine the maximum constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a_{i}$:
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} > C.
$$
solution:
We'll use Hölder's inequality:
If $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} ; b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ and $p, q \in(0,1), 1 / p+1 / q=1$ then we have
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} b_{i} \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{p}\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}^{q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}}
$$

We have
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{3}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} a_{i}^{2} \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{5 / 3}\right)^{3 / 5}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(a_{i}^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}\right)^{2 / 5}
$$
i.e.
$$
\begin{equation*}
3 \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{5 / 3}\right)^{3 / 5} \cdot 5^{2 / 5} \quad \text { i.e. } \quad \frac{3}{5^{2 / 5}} \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{5 / 3}\right)^{3 / 5} \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

We'll show that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{5 / 3} \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}\right)^{5 / 3}
$$

Let $S=\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}$.
Since $0<\frac{a_{i}}{S} \leq 1$ and $\frac{5}{3}>1$ we have that $\left(\frac{a_{i}}{S}\right)^{5 / 3} \leq \frac{a_{i}}{S}=1$ from which we deduce
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{a_{i}}{S}\right)^{5 / 3} \leq \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{a_{i}}{S}=1
$$

So
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{5 / 3} \leq S^{5 / 3}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}\right)^{5 / 3}
$$
since $2^{5}>5^{2}, 2>5^{2 / 5}$ and by (1) we obtain the required inequality.

Equality in the above inequalities holds when all $a_i$ are equal, i.e., $a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_n$. In this case, substituting $a_i = t$ and using the constraints $n t^3 = 3$ and $n t^5 = 5$, we find $t = \left(\frac{3}{n}\right)^{1/3}$ and $t = \left(\frac{5}{n}\right)^{1/5}$, which gives $n = 2$ and $a_1 = a_2 = \frac{3}{2}$. Thus, the minimum value of $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$ is $\frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{2} = 3$, but since the problem asks for the maximum constant $C$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i > C$ always holds, the sharp bound is $C = \frac{3}{2}$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{3}{2}$.

Then

Equality occurs if and only if $\frac{a_{1}^{p}}{b_{1}^{q}}=\frac{a_{2}^{p}}{b_{2}^{q}}=\cdots=\frac{a_{n}^{p}}{b_{n}^{q}}$.

problem:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be positive real numbers. Find the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$:
$$
\frac{a_{1}^{3}}{a_{2}}+\frac{a_{2}^{3}}{a_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{a_{n}^{3}}{a_{1}} \geq C(a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\cdots+a_{n}^{2})
$$
solution:
Let $x_{i} = \ln a_{i}$. Then the given inequality becomes
$$
e^{3 x_{1}-x_{2}}+e^{3 x_{2}-x_{3}}+\cdots+e^{3 x_{n}-x_{1}} \geq e^{2 x_{1}}+e^{2 x_{2}}+\cdots+e^{2 x_{n}}
$$

Let us consider the sequences $a: 3 x_{1}-x_{2}, 3 x_{2}-x_{3}, \ldots, 3 x_{n}-x_{1}$ and $b$ : $2 x_{1}, 2 x_{2}, \ldots, 2 x_{n}$.

Since $f(x)=e^{x}$ is a convex function on $\mathbb{R}$ by Karamata's inequality it suffices to prove that $a$ (ordered in some way) majorizes the sequences $b$ (ordered in some way).

For that purpose, let us assume that
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 3 x_{m_{1}}-x_{m_{1}+1} \geq 3 x_{m_{2}}-x_{m_{2}+1} \geq \cdots \geq 3 x_{m_{n}}-x_{m_{n}+1} \quad \text { and } \\
& 2 x_{k_{1}} \geq 2 x_{k_{2}} \geq \cdots \geq 2 x_{k_{n}}
\end{aligned}
$$
for some indexes $m_{i}, k_{i} \in\{1,2, \ldots, n\}$
Clearly
$$
3 x_{m_{1}}-x_{m_{1}+1} \geq 3 x_{k_{1}}-x_{k_{1}+1} \geq 2 x_{k_{1}}
$$
and
$\left(3 x_{m_{1}}-x_{m_{1}+1}\right)+\left(3 x_{m_{2}}-x_{m_{2}+1}\right) \geq\left(3 x_{k_{1}}-x_{k_{1}+1}\right)+\left(3 x_{k_{2}}-x_{k_{2}+1}\right) \geq 2 x_{k_{1}}+2 x_{k_{2}}$.
Analogously the sum of the first $s$ terms of (a) is not less than the sum of an arbitrary $s$ terms of (a), hence it is not less than $\left(3 x_{k_{1}}-x_{k_{1}+1}\right)+\left(3 x_{k_{2}}-x_{k_{2}+1}\right)+\cdots+$ ( $3 x_{k_{s}}-x_{k_{s}+1}$ ), which, on the other hand, is not less than $2 x_{k_{1}}+2 x_{k_{2}}+\cdots+2 x_{k_{s}}$.

So $a \succ b$, and we are done.

Equality holds when all $a_i$ are equal, i.e., $a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_n$. In this case, both sides of the inequality are equal, and $C = 1$ gives the maximal value for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $a + b + c = 3$. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
\frac{a^{3}}{b(2 c+a)}+\frac{b^{3}}{c(2 a+b)}+\frac{c^{3}}{a(2 b+c)} \geq C
$$
solution:
We'll show that
$$
\frac{a^{3}}{b(2 c+a)}+\frac{b^{3}}{c(2 a+b)}+\frac{c^{3}}{a(2 b+c)} \geq \frac{a+b+c}{3}
$$
from which, with the initial condition, will follow the desired inequality.
Using $A M \geq G M$ we get
$$
\frac{9 a^{3}}{b(2 c+a)}+3 b+(2 c+a) \geq 3 \sqrt[3]{\frac{9 a^{3}}{b(2 c+a)} \cdot 3 b \cdot(2 c+a)}=9 a
$$

Analogously we have
$$
\frac{9 b^{3}}{c(2 a+b)}+3 c+(2 a+b) \geq 3 b \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{9 c^{3}}{a(2 b+c)}+3 a+(2 b+c) \geq 3 c
$$

Adding the last three inequalities we obtain
$$
9\left(\frac{a^{3}}{b(2 c+a)}+\frac{b^{3}}{c(2 a+b)}+\frac{c^{3}}{a(2 b+c)}\right)+6(a+b+c) \geq 9(a+b+c)
$$
i.e.
$$
\frac{a^{3}}{b(2 c+a)}+\frac{b^{3}}{c(2 a+b)}+\frac{c^{3}}{a(2 b+c)} \geq \frac{a+b+c}{3}=\frac{3}{3}=1
$$

Equality holds when $a = b = c = 1$, since then each term is $\frac{1}{1 \cdot (2 \cdot 1 + 1)} = \frac{1}{3}$, and the sum is $3 \times \frac{1}{3} = 1$. This gives the minimum value of the expression, so $C = 1$ is the largest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c \in (0,1)$ be positive real numbers such that $ab + bc + ca = 1$. Find the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$:
$$
\frac{a}{1-a^2} + \frac{b}{1-b^2} + \frac{c}{1-c^2} \geq C \left( \frac{1-a^2}{a} + \frac{1-b^2}{b} + \frac{1-c^2}{c} \right)
$$
solution:
Since $a b+b c+c a=1$ and by Case 3, we use the following substitutions
$$
a=\tan \frac{\alpha}{2}, \quad b=\tan \frac{\beta}{2}, \quad c=\tan \frac{\gamma}{2}
$$
where $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are the angles of a triangle.
Since $a, b, c \in(0,1)$, it follows that $\tan \frac{\alpha}{2}, \tan \frac{\beta}{2}, \tan \frac{\gamma}{2} \in(0,1)$, i.e. it follows that $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are the angles of an acute triangle.

Also we have
$$
\frac{a}{1-a^{2}}=\frac{\tan \frac{\alpha}{2}}{1-\tan ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}}=\frac{\sin \frac{\alpha}{2} \cdot \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}}{\cos \alpha}=\frac{\sin \alpha}{2 \cos \alpha}=\frac{\tan \alpha}{2}
$$

Similarly
$$
\frac{b}{1-b^{2}}=\frac{\tan \beta}{2} \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{c}{1-c^{2}}=\frac{\tan \gamma}{2}
$$

Therefore the given inequality becomes
$$
\frac{\tan \alpha+\tan \beta+\tan \gamma}{2} \geq \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{2}{\tan \alpha}+\frac{2}{\tan \beta}+\frac{2}{\tan \gamma}\right)
$$
or
$$
\begin{equation*}
\tan \alpha+\tan \beta+\tan \gamma \geq 3\left(\frac{1}{\tan \alpha}+\frac{1}{\tan \beta}+\frac{1}{\tan \gamma}\right)
\end{equation*}
$$

By $I_{6}$ we have that $\tan \alpha+\tan \beta+\tan \gamma=\tan \alpha \cdot \tan \beta \cdot \tan \gamma$. Thus it suffices to show that
$$
\begin{aligned}
& (\tan \alpha+\tan \beta+\tan \gamma)^{2} \geq 3(\tan \alpha \tan \beta+\tan \beta \tan \gamma+\tan \gamma \tan \alpha) \\
& \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2}\left((\tan \alpha-\tan \beta)^{2}+(\tan \beta-\tan \gamma)^{2}+(\tan \gamma-\tan \alpha)^{2}\right) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

We are done.

Equality holds when $a = b = c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, which corresponds to $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 60^\circ$ (an equilateral triangle). In this case, both sides of the inequality are equal, so the maximum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = \frac{3}{4}$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{3}{4}$.

theorems.Theorem:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in(0, \pi)$. Then $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are the angles of a triangle if and only if
$$
\sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}+\sin ^{2} \frac{\beta}{2}+\sin ^{2} \frac{\gamma}{2}+2 \sin \frac{\alpha}{2} \cdot \sin \frac{\beta}{2} \cdot \sin \frac{\gamma}{2}=1
$$

problem:
Find the maximum value of the constant $c$ such that for any $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}, \cdots>0$ for which $x_{k+1} \geq x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{k}$ for any $k$, the inequality

$$
\sqrt{x_{1}}+\sqrt{x_{2}}+\cdots+\sqrt{x_{n}} \leq c \sqrt{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}
$$

also holds for any $n$.
solution:
First, let us see what happens if $x_{k+1}$ and $x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{k}$ are close for any $k$. For example, we can take $x_{k}=2^{k}$, because in this case we have $x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{k}=x_{k+1}-2$. Thus, we find that

$$
c \geq \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n} \sqrt{2}^{k}}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{n} 2^{k}}}
$$

for any $n$. Taking the limit, we find that $c \geq 1+\sqrt{2}$. Now, let us prove that $1+\sqrt{2}$ works. We will prove the inequality

$$
\sqrt{x_{1}}+\sqrt{x_{2}}+\cdots+\sqrt{x_{n}} \leq(1+\sqrt{2}) \sqrt{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}
$$

by induction. For $n=1$ or $n=2$ it is clear. Suppose it is true for $n$ and we will prove that $\sqrt{x_{1}}+\sqrt{x_{2}}+\cdots+\sqrt{x_{n}}+\sqrt{x_{n+1}} \leq(1+\sqrt{2}) \sqrt{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}+x_{n+1}}$. Of course, it is enough to prove that

$$
\sqrt{x_{n+1}} \leq(1+\sqrt{2})\left(\sqrt{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n+1}}-\sqrt{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}\right)
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\sqrt{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}+\sqrt{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n+1}} \leq(1+\sqrt{2}) \sqrt{x_{n+1}}
$$

But this one follows because

$$
x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n} \leq x_{n+1}
$$

Equality holds when the sequence is chosen so that $x_{k+1} = x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k$ for all $k$, for example, when $x_k = 2^k$. In this case, the ratio approaches $1+\sqrt{2}$ as $n$ grows, so this gives the maximum value of $c$.

Therefore, the answer is $c = 1+\sqrt{2}$.

problem:
Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that $xyz = x + y + z + 2$. Find the smallest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x, y, z$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z} \leq C \sqrt{xyz}
$$
solution:
The given inequality is equivalent to
$$
\begin{align*}
& \frac{1}{\sqrt{y z}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z x}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x y}} \leq \frac{3}{2} \\
& \quad \Leftrightarrow \sqrt{\frac{a}{b+c} \cdot \frac{b}{c+a}}+\sqrt{\frac{b}{c+a} \cdot \frac{c}{a+b}}+\sqrt{\frac{c}{a+b} \cdot \frac{a}{b+c}} \leq \frac{3}{2} \tag{1}
\end{align*}
$$

Using $A M \geq G M$ we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sqrt{\frac{a}{b+c} \cdot \frac{b}{c+a}} \leq \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{a}{a+c}+\frac{b}{c+b}\right) \\
& \sqrt{\frac{b}{c+a} \cdot \frac{c}{a+b}} \leq \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{b}{a+b}+\frac{c}{c+a}\right) \text { and } \\
& \sqrt{\frac{c}{a+b} \cdot \frac{a}{b+c}} \leq \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{c}{b+c}+\frac{a}{a+b}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the last three inequalities we obtain inequality (1), as required.

Equality holds when $x = y = z = 2$, since then $xyz = 8$ and $x + y + z + 2 = 8$, so the constraint is satisfied, and $\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z} = 3 \cdot \sqrt{2}$, $C \sqrt{xyz} = C \cdot 2\sqrt{2}$. Setting $3\sqrt{2} = C \cdot 2\sqrt{2}$ gives $C = \frac{3}{2}$. This gives the minimum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{3}{2}$.

problem:
Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that $xy + yz + zx = 5$. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x, y, z$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
3x^2 + 3y^2 + z^2 \geq C
$$
solution:
Using the inequality $A M \geq G M$ we obtain
$$
4 x^{2}+z^{2} \geq 4 x z, \quad 4 y^{2}+z^{2} \geq 4 y z \quad \text { and } \quad 2 x^{2}+2 y^{2} \geq 4 x y
$$

Adding these inequalities and using $x y+y z+z x=5$ we get the required inequality.
Equality occurs iff $x=y=1, z=2$.

Equality is achieved when $x = y = 1$ and $z = 2$, which also satisfies $xy + yz + zx = 5$. In this case, $3x^2 + 3y^2 + z^2 = 3(1^2) + 3(1^2) + (2^2) = 3 + 3 + 4 = 10$. Thus, the minimum value of $3x^2 + 3y^2 + z^2$ is $10$, so the largest constant $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = 10$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 10$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be the lengths of the sides of a triangle with area $P$. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} \geq C P
$$
solution:
After setting $a=x+y, b=y+z, c=z+x$ where $x, y, z>0$, the given inequality becomes
$$
\left((x+y)^{2}+(y+z)^{2}+(z+x)^{2}\right)^{2} \geq 48 x y z(x+y+z)
$$

From $A M \geq G M$ we have
$$
\begin{equation*}
\left((x+y)^{2}+(y+z)^{2}+(z+x)^{2}\right)^{2} \geq(4 x y+4 y z+4 z x)^{2}=16(x y+y z+z x)^{2} \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since for every $p, q, r \in \mathbb{R}$ we have $(p+q+r)^{2} \geq 3(p q+q r+r p)$, by (1) we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left((x+y)^{2}+(y+z)^{2}+(z+x)^{2}\right)^{2} \\
& \quad \geq 16(x y+y z+z x)^{2} \\
& \quad \geq 16 \cdot 3((x y)(y z)+(y z)(z x)+(z x)(x y))=48 x y z(x+y+z)
\end{aligned}
$$
as required.

Equality holds when $x = y = z$, which corresponds to $a = b = c$, i.e., the triangle is equilateral. In this case, the value $C = 4\sqrt{3}$ gives the maximum possible value for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 4\sqrt{3}$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c, x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
(a+b+c)(x+y+z)=4
$$
and
$$
(a^2+b^2+c^2)(x^2+y^2+z^2)=4.
$$
Find the smallest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c, x, y, z$ satisfying the given constraints:
$$
abcxyz < C.
$$
solution:
Using the AM-GM Inequality, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
4(a b+b c+c a)(x y+y z+z x)=\left[(a+b+c)^{2}-\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)\right]\left[(x+y+z)^{2}-\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)\right]= \\
=20-(a+b+c)^{2}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)-\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)(x+y+z)^{2} \leq \\
\leq 20-2 \sqrt{(a+b+c)^{2}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)(x+y+z)^{2}}=4
\end{gathered}
$$

therefore

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a b+b c+c a)(x y+y z+z a) \leq 1 \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

By multiplying the well-known inequalities

$$
(a b+b c+c a)^{2} \geq 3 a b c(a+b+c), \quad(x y+y z+z x)^{2} \geq 3 x y z(x+y+z)
$$

it follows that

$$
(a b+b c+c a)^{2}(x y+y z+z x)^{2} \geq 9 a b c x y z(a+b+c)(x+y+z)
$$

or

$$
\begin{equation*}
(a b+b c+c a)(x y+y z+z x) \geq 36 a b c x y z \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

From (1) and (2), we conclude that

$$
1 \leq(a b+b c+c a)(x y+y z+z x) \geq 36 a b c x y z
$$

therefore $1 \leq 36 a b c x y z$.
To have $1=36 a b c x y z$, the equalities $(a b+b c+c a)^{2}=3 a b c(a+b+c)$ and $(x y+y z+z x)^{2}=3 x y z(x+y+z)$ are necessary. But these conditions imply $a=b=c$ and $x=y=z$, which contradict the relations $(a+b+c)(x+y+z)=\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+\right.$ $\left.c^{2}\right)\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)=4$. Thus, it follows that $1>36 a b c x y z$.

Equality in the above inequalities would require $a = b = c$ and $x = y = z$, but this is not possible under the given constraints $(a+b+c)(x+y+z) = (a^2+b^2+c^2)(x^2+y^2+z^2) = 4$. Therefore, the maximum possible value of $abcxyz$ is strictly less than $\frac{1}{36}$, and $C = \frac{1}{36}$ is the smallest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{1}{36}$.

problem:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $a b + b c + a c = 1$. Find the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
\frac{1 + a^2 b^2}{(a + b)^2} + \frac{1 + b^2 c^2}{(b + c)^2} + \frac{1 + c^2 a^2}{(c + a)^2} \geq C
$$
solution:
The given inequality is equivalent to
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{c y c} \frac{(a b+b c+a c)^{2}+a^{2} b^{2}}{(a+b)^{2}} \geq \frac{5}{2}(a b+b c+a c) \\
& \Leftrightarrow \quad 2 \sum_{c y c} \frac{2 a b(a b+b c+a c)+(b c+c a)^{2}}{(a+b)^{2}} \geq 5(a b+b c+a c) \\
& \Leftrightarrow \quad 4(a b+b c+c a)\left(\frac{a b}{(a+b)^{2}}+\frac{b c}{(b+c)^{2}}+\frac{c a}{(c+a)^{2}}\right) \\
& \quad+2\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right) \geq 5(a b+b c+a c) \\
& \Leftrightarrow \quad(a b+b c+c a)\left(\frac{4 a b}{(a+b)^{2}}+\frac{4 b c}{(b+c)^{2}}+\frac{4 c a}{(c+a)^{2}}-3\right) \\
& \quad+2\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-a b-b c-c a\right) \geq 0 \\
& \Leftrightarrow-(a b+b c+c a)\left(\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{(a+b)^{2}}+\frac{(b-c)^{2}}{(b+c)^{2}}+\frac{(c-a)^{2}}{(c+a)^{2}}\right) \\
& \quad+\left((a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}+(c-a)^{2}\right) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Leftrightarrow \quad & \left(1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(a+b)^{2}}\right)(a-b)^{2}+\left(1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(b+c)^{2}}\right)(b-c)^{2} \\
& +\left(1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(c+a)^{2}}\right)(c-a)^{2} \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Let
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S_{a}=1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(b+c)^{2}}, \quad S_{b}=1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(c+a)^{2}} \quad \text { and } \\
& S_{c}=1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(a+b)^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Without loss of generality we may assume that $a \geq b \geq c$, and then clearly $S_{a} \leq S_{b} \leq S_{c}$.

We have
$$
S_{c}=1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(a+b)^{2}}=\frac{a^{2}+(a+b)(b-c)}{(a+b)^{2}}>0
$$
and it follows that $S_{b} \geq S_{c}>0$.
Also we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{2} S_{b}+b^{2} S_{a} & =a^{2}\left(1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(c+a)^{2}}\right)+b^{2}\left(1-\frac{a b+b c+c a}{(b+c)^{2}}\right) \\
& =a^{2} \frac{c^{2}+(c+a)(a-b)}{(c+a)^{2}}+b^{2} \frac{c^{2}+(b+c)(b-a)}{(b+c)^{2}} \\
& =c^{2}\left(\frac{a^{2}}{(c+a)^{2}}+\frac{b^{2}}{(b+c)^{2}}\right)+(a-b)\left(\frac{a^{2}}{c+a}-\frac{b^{2}}{b+c}\right) \\
& =(a-b)^{2} \frac{a b+b c+c a}{(c+a)(b+c)}+c^{2}\left(\frac{a^{2}}{(c+a)^{2}}+\frac{b^{2}}{(b+c)^{2}}\right)>0
\end{aligned}
$$
and we are done.
Equality occurs iff $a=b=c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

Equality in the above holds when $a = b = c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, since then $ab + bc + ca = 3 \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = 1$, and each term in the sum becomes $\frac{1 + (1/3)}{(2/\sqrt{3})^2} = \frac{4/3}{4/3} = 1$, so the sum is $3 \times 1 = 3$. Plugging into the original inequality, we get $3 \geq C$, and the calculations above show that $C = \frac{5}{2}$ is the maximal value for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{5}{2}$.

problem:
Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = xyz$. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x, y, z$ satisfying the given constraint:
$$
xy + yz + zx \geq C
$$
solution:
Using $A M \geq G M$ we get
$$
x y z=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} \geq 3 \sqrt[3]{(x y z)^{2}}, \text { i.e. }(x y z)^{3} \geq 27(x y z)^{2}
$$
which implies
$$
x y z \geq 27
$$
By $A M \geq G M$ we get $x y+y z+z x \geq 3 \sqrt[3]{(x y z)^{2}} \geq 3 \sqrt[3]{27^{2}}=27$.

Equality holds when $x = y = z = 3$, since then $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 3 \times 9 = 27 = xyz$, and $xy + yz + zx = 3 \times 9 = 27$. This gives the minimum value of $xy + yz + zx$, so $C = 27$ is the largest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 27$.

problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ and $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be positive real numbers satisfying

$$
\frac{1}{x_{1}+1998}+\frac{1}{x_{2}+1998}+\ldots+\frac{1}{x_{n}+1998}=\frac{1}{1998}
$$

Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}$:

\frac{\sqrt[n]{x_{1} x_{2} \ldots x_{n}}}{n-1} \geq C
$$

Let $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$. Find the smallest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $x, y, z$:
$$
(x+y+z)^{2}(x y+y z+z x)^{2} \leq C\left(x^{2}+x y+y^{2}\right)\left(y^{2}+y z+z^{2}\right)\left(z^{2}+z x+x^{2}\right)
$$
solution:
We have
$$
x^{2}+x y+y^{2}=\frac{3}{4}(x+y)^{2}+\frac{1}{4}(x-y)^{2} \geq \frac{3}{4}(x+y)^{2}
$$
similarly
$$
y^{2}+y z+z^{2} \geq \frac{3}{4}(y+z)^{2} \quad \text { and } \quad z^{2}+z x+x^{2} \geq \frac{3}{4}(z+x)^{2}
$$

Hence
$$
\begin{aligned}
3\left(x^{2}+x y+y^{2}\right)\left(y^{2}+y z+z^{2}\right)\left(z^{2}+z x+x^{2}\right) & \geq 3\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{3}(x+y)^{2}(y+z)^{2}(z+x)^{2} \\
& =\frac{81}{64}((x+y)(y+z)(z+x))^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We'll show that
$$
\frac{81}{64}((x+y)(y+z)(z+x))^{2} \geq(x+y+z)^{2}(x y+y z+z x)^{2}
$$
i.e.
$$
\frac{9}{8}(x+y)(y+z)(z+x) \geq(x+y+z)(x y+y z+z x)
$$
i.e.
$$
\begin{equation*}
9(x+y)(y+z)(z+x) \geq 8(x+y+z)(x y+y z+z x) \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$
from which we'll obtain the desired inequality.
Let's note that
$$
(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)=(x+y+z)(x y+y z+z x)-x y z .
$$

Now by (1) we get
$$
9(x+y)(y+z)(z+x) \geq 8((x+y)(y+z)(z+x)+x y z)
$$
i.e.
$$
(x+y)(y+z)(z+x) \geq 8 x y z
$$
which is clearly true since
$$
x+y \geq 2 \sqrt{x y}, \quad y+z \geq 2 \sqrt{y z}, \quad z+x \geq 2 \sqrt{z x} .
$$

Equality occurs if and only if $x = y = z$, in which case both sides of the original inequality are equal. This gives the minimum value of $C$, so $C = 3$ is the smallest constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 3$.

problem:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the angles of a triangle. Find the largest constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ satisfying $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = \pi$ and $0 < \alpha, \beta, \gamma < \pi$:
$$
\sin \alpha + \sin \beta + \sin \gamma \geq C (\sin 2\alpha + \sin 2\beta + \sin 2\gamma)
$$
solution:
Applying the sine law we obtain
$$
sin \alpha+\sin \beta+\sin \gamma=\frac{a+b+c}{2 R}=\frac{P}{r R}
$$

Also
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin 2 \alpha+\sin 2 \beta+\sin 2 \gamma & =2(\sin \alpha \cos \alpha+\sin \beta \cos \beta+\sin \gamma \cos \gamma) \\
& =\frac{1}{R}(a \cos \alpha+b \cos \beta+c \cos \gamma)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since
$$
a \cos \alpha+b \cos \beta+c \cos \gamma=\frac{2 P}{R}
$$
we have
$$
\sin 2 \alpha+\sin 2 \beta+\sin 2 \gamma=\frac{2 P}{R^{2}}
$$

Therefore
$$
\frac{\sin \alpha+\sin \beta+\sin \gamma}{\sin 2 \alpha+\sin 2 \beta+\sin 2 \gamma}=\frac{R}{2 r} \geq 1
$$

Equality holds if and only if the triangle is equilateral, that is, when $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = \frac{\pi}{3}$. This gives the minimum value of $\frac{\sin \alpha+\sin \beta+\sin \gamma}{\sin 2 \alpha+\sin 2 \beta+\sin 2 \sin 2 \gamma}$, so the largest constant $C$ is $1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.
