problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c, x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$:
$$
\frac{x}{y+z}(b+c)+\frac{y}{z+x}(c+a)+\frac{z}{x+y}(a+b) \geqslant C\sqrt{ab+bc+ca}.
$$
solution:
11. Let $\sum$ denote cyclic sum.

Notice that,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\sum \frac{x}{y+z}(b+c) \\
=(x+y+z) \sum \frac{b+c}{y+z}-2(a+b+c) \\
=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum(x+y)\right)\left(\sum \frac{b+c}{y+z}\right)-2(a+b+c) \\
\geqslant \frac{1}{2}\left(\sum \sqrt{a+b}\right)^{2}-2(a+b+c) \\
=\sum \sqrt{(a+b)(a+c)}-(a+b+c) .
\end{array}
$$

We now prove that
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\sum \sqrt{(a+b)(a+c)}-(a+b+c) \\
\geqslant \sqrt{3(a b+b c+c a)} .
\end{array}
$$

By $\sqrt{(a+b)(a+c)}-a$
$$
=\frac{a b+b c+c a}{\sqrt{(a+b)(a+c)}+a} \text {, }
$$

we know that inequality (1)
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Leftrightarrow & (\sqrt{a b+b c+c a}) \sum \frac{1}{\sqrt{(a+b)(a+c)}+a} \\
& \geqslant \sqrt{3} .
\end{aligned}
$$

By homogeneity, we may assume $a b+b c+c a=1$.
Let $a=\cot A, b=\cot B, c=\cot C$, where,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\angle A & +\angle B+\angle C=\pi . \\
& \text { Then } \sum \frac{1}{\sqrt{(a+b)(a+c)}+a}=\sum \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}+1}+a} \\
& =\sum \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\sin A}+\cot A}=\sum \frac{\sin A}{1+\cos A} \\
& =\sum \tan \frac{A}{2} . \\
& \text { Also }\left(\sum \tan \frac{A}{2}\right)^{2} \geqslant 3 \sum\left(\tan \frac{A}{2} \cdot \tan \frac{B}{2}\right)=3,
\end{aligned}
$$

hence inequality (1) holds.

Equality holds when $a = b = c$, and $x = y = z$, that is, when all variables are equal. In this case, the left side and right side of the inequality are equal, and $C$ attains its maximal value $\sqrt{3}$. Therefore, this gives the maximum value of $C$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \sqrt{3}.$.

problem:
Determine the largest real constant C such that for any positive integer n, and any sequences of positive real numbers x_1, ..., x_n and y_1, ..., y_n, and any sequence of positive real numbers z_1, ..., z_{2n} satisfying z_{i+j}^2 ≥ x_i y_j for all 1 ≤ i, j ≤ n, with M = \max\{z_2, z_3, ..., z_{2n}\}, the following inequality holds:
\[
\left(\frac{M + z_2 + z_3 + \cdots + z_{2n}}{2n}\right)^2 \geq C \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}\right)\left(\frac{y_1 + y_2 + \cdots + y_n}{n}\right).
\]
solution:
6. Let $X=\max \left\{x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right\}, Y=\max \left\{y_{1}, y_{2}, \cdots, y_{n}\right\}$. Replace $x_{i}$ with $x_{i}^{\prime}=\frac{x_{i}}{X}$, $y_{i}$ with $y^{\prime}_{i}=\frac{y_{i}}{Y}$, and $z_{i}$ with $z^{\prime}_{i}=\frac{z_{i}}{\sqrt{X Y}}$, then the original inequality remains unchanged. Without loss of generality, assume $X=Y=1$, and we will prove
$$
M+z_{2}+z_{3}+\cdots+z_{2 n} \geqslant x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}+y_{1}+y_{2}+\cdots+y_{n}.
$$

It suffices to show that for any $r \geqslant 0$, the number of terms on the left side of (1) that are greater than $r$ is no less than the number of terms on the right side that are greater than $r$.
If $r \geqslant 1$, then there are no terms on the right side that are greater than $r$, so assume $r < 1$. Let
$$
A=\left\{i \mid x_{i}>r, 1 \leqslant i \leqslant n\right\}, a=|A|,
$$
$$
B=\left\{i \mid y_{i}>r, 1 \leqslant i \leqslant n\right\}, b=|B|.
$$
Since $\max \left\{x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right\}=\max \left\{y_{1}, y_{2}, \cdots, y_{n}\right\}=1$, then $a$ and $b$ are at least 1. From $x_{i}>r, y_{i}>r$, we get $z_{i+j} \geqslant \sqrt{x_{i} y_{j}}>r$, so,
$$
C=\left\{i \mid z_{i}>r, 2 \leqslant i \leqslant 2 n\right\} \supset(A+B)=\{\alpha+\beta \mid \alpha \in A, \beta \in B\}.
$$

Let $A=\left\{i_{1}, i_{2}, \cdots, i_{a}\right\}, i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{a}$, and $B=\left\{j_{1}, j_{2}, \cdots, j_{b}\right\}, j_{1}<j_{2}<\cdots<j_{b}$. Then, for any $1 \leqslant k \leqslant a, 1 \leqslant l \leqslant b$, we have $i_{k}+j_{l} \leqslant i_{a}+j_{b} \leqslant 2 n$, and $z_{i_{k}+j_{l}}>r$.
Since $M>r$, the left side of (1) has at least $a+b$ terms greater than $r$. Since $a+b$ is the number of terms on the right side that are greater than $r$, the conclusion holds. Therefore,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(\frac{M+z_{2}+z_{3}+\cdots+z_{2 n}}{2 n}\right)^{2} & \geqslant\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}{n}+\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+\cdots+y_{n}}{n}\right)\right]^{2} \\
& \geqslant\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}{n}\right)\left(\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+\cdots+y_{n}}{n}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Equality holds when all $x_i$ and $y_j$ are equal, and all $z_k$ are equal as well, for example when $x_i = y_j = 1$ for all $i, j$, and $z_k = 1$ for all $k$. In this case, both sides of the inequality are equal, so $C = 1$ is the largest possible value. This gives the minimum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1.$.

problem:
(1) Determine the maximal real constant $C$ such that for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $|\sin x \pm \cos x| \leq C$.

(2) Determine the maximal and minimal real constants $C_1$ and $C_2$ such that for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $C_1 \leq |\sin x| + |\cos x| \leq C_2$.
solution:
Prove (1) Calculation yields
$$
sin x \pm \cos x=\sqrt{2} \sin \left(x \pm \frac{\pi}{4}\right) .
$$

Since
$$
-1 \leqslant \sin \left(x \pm \frac{\pi}{4}\right) \leqslant 1,
$$

it follows that
$$
-\sqrt{2} \leqslant \sin x \pm \cos x \leqslant \sqrt{2} \text {. }
$$
(2) This part can be solved by discussing to remove the absolute value signs, thereby reducing it to the form of the previous part. However, if the square method is used to remove the absolute value signs, the cumbersome discussion can be avoided. Because
$$
\begin{aligned}
(|\sin x|+|\cos x|)^{2} & =1+2|\sin x||\cos x| \\
& =1+|\sin 2 x|,
\end{aligned}
$$

and $0 \leqslant|\sin 2 x| \leqslant 1$, so
$$
1 \leqslant(|\sin x|+|\cos x|)^{2} \leqslant 2,
$$

thus
$$
1 \leqslant|\sin x|+|\cos x| \leqslant \sqrt{2} \text {. }
$$

Equality in (1) holds when $x \pm \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$ for some integer $k$, i.e., when $\sin x \pm \cos x = \pm\sqrt{2}$. Thus, the maximum value of $C$ is $\sqrt{2}$.

For (2), $|\sin x| + |\cos x|$ achieves its minimum $1$ when $|\sin x| = 0$ or $|\cos x| = 0$, i.e., $x = k\pi$ or $x = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, and its maximum $\sqrt{2}$ when $|\sin x| = |\cos x| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, i.e., $x = \frac{\pi}{4} + k\frac{\pi}{2}$ for integer $k$.

Therefore, the answer is $(1) $C = \sqrt{2}$.
(2) $C_1 = 1$, $C_2 = \sqrt{2}$.$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ with $x \neq y$, the following inequality holds:
$$
(\cos x-\cos y)^2+(\sin x-\sin y)^2 < C(x-y)^2.
$$
solution:
According to the addition theorems, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\cos x-\cos y)^{2}+(\sin x-\sin y)^{2} & =\left(\cos ^{2} x+\sin ^{2} x\right)+\left(\cos ^{2} y+\sin ^{2} y\right)-2(\cos x \cos y+\sin x \sin y)= \\
& =2-2 \cos (x-y)=4 \sin ^{2} \frac{x-y}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

(the latter due to $1-\cos x=2 \sin ^{2} \frac{x}{2}$). The sine function has the property $|\sin x|<|x|$ for $x \neq 0$; since $x \neq y$, it follows that $x-y \neq 0$ and we get

$$
4 \sin ^{2} \frac{x-y}{2}<4\left(\frac{x-y}{2}\right)^{2}=(x-y)^{2}
$$

Thus, the proof is complete.

Equality is never achieved for $x \neq y$ because $|\sin t| < |t|$ for all $t \neq 0$, so the inequality is always strict. The value $C = 1$ is the maximal constant for which the inequality holds for all $x \neq y$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Determine the minimal constant $C$ such that for any triangle $ABC$ and any internal point $M$, with $A_1 = AM \cap BC$, $B_1 = BM \cap CA$, and $C_1 = CM \cap AB$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\frac{\overline{AM}}{\overline{A_1M}} + \frac{\overline{BM}}{\overline{B_1M}} + \frac{\overline{CM}}{\overline{C_1M}} \geq C.
$$
solution:
Solution. Let $S$ be the area of $\triangle ABC$, and $S_{1}, S_{2}, S_{3}$ be the areas of $\triangle MBC, \triangle MCA, \triangle MAB$ respectively. Triangles $ABC$ and $MBC$ have the same base, so it follows that

$$
\overline{A A_{1}}: \overline{M A_{1}}=S: S_{1}=\left(S_{1}+S_{2}+S_{3}\right): S_{1}
$$

From this,

$$
\left(\overline{A A_{1}}-\overline{M A_{1}}\right): \overline{M A_{1}}=\left(S_{2}+S_{3}\right): S_{1}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_06_05_e8e81a1ae01081700bfcg-4.jpg?height=414&width=560&top_left_y=716&top_left_x=919)
which means $\frac{\overline{M A}}{\overline{M A_{1}}}=\frac{S_{2}}{S_{1}}+\frac{S_{3}}{S_{1}}$. Similarly, $\frac{\overline{M B}}{\overline{M B}}=\frac{S_{1}}{S_{3}}+\frac{S_{2}}{S_{3}}$ and $\frac{\overline{M C}}{\overline{M C_{1}}}=\frac{S_{1}}{S_{2}}+\frac{S_{3}}{S_{2}}$. Therefore,

$$
\frac{\overline{A M}}{\overline{A_{1} M}}+\frac{\overline{B M}}{\overline{B_{1} M}}+\frac{\overline{C M}}{\overline{C_{1} M}}=\left(\frac{S_{1}}{S_{2}}+\frac{S_{2}}{S_{1}}\right)+\left(\frac{S_{2}}{S_{3}}+\frac{S_{3}}{S_{2}}\right)+\left(\frac{S_{3}}{S_{1}}+\frac{S_{1}}{S_{3}}\right) \geq 2 \sqrt{\frac{S_{1}}{S_{2}} \frac{S_{2}}{S_{1}}}+2 \sqrt{\frac{S_{2}}{S_{3}} \frac{S_{3}}{S_{2}}}+2 \sqrt{\frac{S_{3}}{S_{1}} \frac{S_{1}}{S_{3}}}=6
$$

Equality holds when $S_1 = S_2 = S_3$, that is, when $M$ is the centroid of triangle $ABC$. In this case, the sum achieves its minimum value, so $C = 6$ is the minimal constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 6$.

Therefore it is enongil to prove $\frac{(a h+b c+c a)^{2}}{6} \leq \frac{(a b+b c+c a)^{2}}{6}$. This mequalits is trivially shomn to be equivalent to $3 \leq a b+b c+c a$ which is true because of the AM-GM inequalit: $3=\sqrt[3]{(a b c)^{2}} \leq a b+b c+c a$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all non-negative real numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ with $x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n = a$, the following inequality holds:
$$
x_1 x_2 + x_2 x_3 + \cdots + x_{n-1} x_n \leq C a^2.
$$
solution:
2. When $n=2,3$, it is obvious that $x_{1} x_{2} \leqslant \frac{\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right)^{2}}{4}=\frac{a^{2}}{4}, x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}=x_{2}\left(x_{1}+x_{3}\right) \leqslant \frac{\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}\right)^{2}}{4}=\frac{a^{2}}{4}$. When $n \geqslant 4$, a stronger inequality can be proven: $x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+\cdots+x_{n-1} x_{n}+x_{n} x_{1} \leqslant \frac{a^{2}}{4}$.

In fact, when $n=4$, since $x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{1}=\left(x_{1}+x_{3}\right)\left(x_{2}+x_{4}\right) \leqslant \frac{a^{2}}{4}$, (1) holds. For any non-negative real numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{k}, x_{k+1}$, by the cyclic symmetry of the left side of (1), we can assume $x_{k+1}=\max \left\{x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{k}, x_{k+1}\right\}$. Let $y_{1}=x_{1}+x_{2}, y_{2}=x_{3}, \cdots, y_{k-1}=x_{k}, y_{k}=x_{k+1}$, then $y_{1}+y_{2}+\cdots+y_{k}=x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{k}+x_{k+1}=a$. By the induction hypothesis, $y_{1} y_{2}+y_{2} y_{3}+\cdots+y_{k-1} y_{k}+y_{k} y_{1} \leqslant \frac{a^{2}}{4}$. Furthermore, $y_{1} y_{2}+y_{k} y_{1}=\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right) x_{3}+x_{k+1}\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right) \geqslant x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+x_{k+1} x_{1}$, thus $x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+\cdots+x_{k} x_{k+1}+x_{k+1} x_{1} \leqslant \frac{a^{2}}{4}$, meaning (1) also holds for $n=k+1$. Therefore, for $n \geqslant 4$, (1) holds.

Equality holds when two of the $x_i$ are equal to $\frac{a}{2}$ and the rest are zero, for example, $x_1 = x_2 = \frac{a}{2}$, $x_3 = \cdots = x_n = 0$. In this case, $x_1 x_2 = \frac{a^2}{4}$ and all other terms are zero, so the sum achieves $\frac{a^2}{4}$. This gives the maximum value of $C$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{1}{4}$.

problem: Determine the largest real constant C such that for all positive numbers u, v, w less than 1, at least one of the numbers u(1-v), v(1-w), w(1-u) is less than or equal to C.
solution:
Indirect Proof: Assume that none of the numbers \(u(1-v), v(1-w), w(1-u)\) is not greater than \(\frac{1}{4}\), i.e., all three numbers are greater than \(\frac{1}{4}\). Their multiplication yields

\[
u v w(1-u)(1-v)(1-w)>\frac{1}{64}\]

On the other hand, \(u(1-u)=\frac{1}{4}-\left(u-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} \leq \frac{1}{4}\); analogous inequalities hold for \(v\) and \(w\). Multiplying these three inequalities shows that (1) does not hold. Therefore, the above assumption is false, and the claim is proven.

Equality holds when one of the variables, say \(u\), equals \(\frac{1}{2}\) and the others approach 1, so that \(u(1-v) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0 = 0\) or when \(u = v = w = \frac{1}{2}\), giving \(u(1-v) = \frac{1}{4}\). Thus, the maximum value of \(C\) for which the statement is always true is \(C = \frac{1}{4}\).

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{1}{4}$.

problem: Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that $C < \cos 20^\circ \cdot \cos 40^\circ \cdot \cos 70^\circ$ holds true. (Equivalently, find the value of $\cos 20^\circ \cdot \cos 40^\circ \cdot \cos 70^\circ$.)
solution:
## Solution.

$\frac{1}{2}<4 \cos 20^{\circ} \cdot \cos 40^{\circ} \cdot \sin 20^{\circ}<1 \Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2}<2 \sin 40^{\circ} \cdot \cos 40^{\circ}<1 \Leftrightarrow$

$\Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2}<\sin 80^{\circ}<1 \Leftrightarrow \sin 30^{\circ}<\sin 80^{\circ}<\sin 90^{\circ}$.

The last statement is obvious.

Equality in $C < \cos 20^\circ \cdot \cos 40^\circ \cdot \cos 70^\circ$ is approached as $C$ tends to $\cos 20^\circ \cdot \cos 40^\circ \cdot \cos 70^\circ$ from below, but never reached. The maximum value of $C$ is $\cos 20^\circ \cdot \cos 40^\circ \cdot \cos 70^\circ = 0.125$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 0.125$.

problem:
Determine the minimal constant $C$ such that for all $x_1,\ldots,x_n > 0$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_n \geq 0$ not all zero, and for all real numbers $0 < p < q$, the following holds:
$$
\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} x_{i}^{p}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}}\right)^{1 / p} \leq C \left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} x_{i}^{q}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}}\right)^{1 / q}
$$
solution:
By replacing $a_{i}$ with $a_{i} / \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}$, we can assume that $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}=1$. We consider $f(x)=x^{q / p}$ which is convex since $q / p \geqslant 1$. By applying Jensen's inequality to the $x_{i}^{p}$ with the coefficients $a_{i}$, we obtain:

$$
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} x_{i}^{p}\right)^{q / p} \leqslant \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}\left(x_{i}^{p}\right)^{q / p}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} x_{i}^{q}
$$

We conclude by taking the $q$-th root of both sides.

Equality holds when all $x_i$ are equal, i.e., $x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n$. In this case, both sides of the inequality are equal, so the minimal constant $C$ is $1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+$ with $x + 2y = 1$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} \geq C.
$$
solution:
Prove that since $x, y \in \mathbf{R}^{+}$, and $x+2 y=1$, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y} & =(x+2 y) \cdot\left(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}\right) \\
& =\frac{x}{y}+\frac{2 y}{x}+3 \geqslant 2 \sqrt{\frac{x}{y} \cdot \frac{2 y}{x}}+3=3+2 \sqrt{2} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Equality holds when $\frac{x}{y} = \frac{2y}{x}$, i.e., when $x = \sqrt{2}y$. Using $x + 2y = 1$, we get $\sqrt{2}y + 2y = 1 \implies y = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} + 2}$ and $x = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2} + 2}$. Thus, the minimum value of $\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y}$ is $3 + 2\sqrt{2}$, so this is the maximal constant $C$ for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 3 + 2\sqrt{2}.$.

problem:
Determine the minimal real constant $C$ such that for every real number $x \geq \frac{1}{2}$, there exists an integer $n$ satisfying
$$
|x^2 - n| \leq C.
$$
solution:
Solution. Let $a_{n} = \frac{(n-1)^{2} + n^{2}}{2},\ n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $a_{1} = \frac{1}{2}$, the sequence $\left(a_{n}\right)$ is monotonically increasing and tends to infinity. For every $x \geq \frac{1}{2}$ there exists a natural number $n$ such that $a_{n-1} \leq x \leq a_{n}$. The last inequalities hold if and only if

$$
f(x) = \left(x - a_{n-1}\right)\left(x - a_{n}\right) = x^{2} - \left(2n^{2} + 1\right)x + \left(n^{4} + \frac{1}{4}\right) = \left(x - n^{2}\right)^{2} - \left(x - \frac{1}{4}\right) \leq 0
$$

from which it follows $\left|x^{2} - n\right| \leq \sqrt{x - \frac{1}{4}}$.

Equality holds when $x = \frac{1}{2}$, since then $\left|x^{2} - n\right| = \left|\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} - 0\right| = \frac{1}{4}$, and $\sqrt{\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$. However, the minimal value of $C$ such that $|x^2 - n| \leq C$ for all $x \geq \frac{1}{2}$ and some integer $n$ is achieved when $x = \frac{1}{2}$ and $n = 0$, giving $C = \frac{1}{4}$. This gives the minimum possible value of $C$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{1}{4}.$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all positive real numbers $x, y, z$, the following inequality holds:
$$
C\left(\frac{x+1}{y+1}+\frac{y+1}{z+1}+\frac{z+1}{x+1}\right) \leq \frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{z}+\frac{z}{x}.
$$
solution:
Solution. Note that $\frac{a+1}{b+1}-\frac{a}{b}=\frac{b-a}{b(b+1)}$ for any positive $a$ and $b$. Therefore, after moving all terms to the left side, the required inequality takes the form

$$
\frac{y-x}{y(y+1)}+\frac{z-y}{z(z+1)}+\frac{x-z}{x(x+1)} \leqslant 0
$$

We can assume that $x$ is the largest of the three given numbers. There are two cases.

Case 1. $y \geqslant z$. In this case, we have

$$
\frac{x-y}{x(x+1)} \leqslant \frac{x-y}{y(y+1)}, \quad \frac{y-z}{x(x+1)} \leqslant \frac{y-z}{z(z+1)}
$$

Adding these inequalities, we get

$$
\frac{x-z}{x(x+1)} \leqslant-\frac{y-x}{y(y+1)}-\frac{z-y}{z(z+1)}
$$

which is equivalent to (1).

Case 2. $y<z$. Then we have

$$
\frac{z-y}{z(z+1)} \leqslant \frac{z-y}{y(y+1)}, \quad \frac{x-z}{x(x+1)} \leqslant \frac{x-z}{y(y+1)}
$$

Adding these inequalities, we get

$$
\frac{z-y}{z(z+1)}+\frac{x-z}{x(x+1)} \leqslant-\frac{y-x}{y(y+1)}
$$

which is again equivalent to (1).

Comment. There are two different ways to order the variables, up to cyclic permutation (in the author's solution, these are the cases $x \geqslant y \geqslant z$ and $x \geqslant z \geqslant y$). Correct consideration of only one of these cases - to award 3 points.

Equality holds when $x = y = z$, in which case both sides of the original inequality are equal and $C = 1$ is achieved. This gives the maximal value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1.$.

with this, we have proven the statement - under the given restrictions.

Thus, in (1), equality holds if and only if the positive numbers are such that the inequality between the arithmetic and geometric means of positive numbers was applied to four equal numbers in both steps. Remark. The statement (1) - without the given restrictions - is obviously not true if all four logarithms are negative. Equality is achieved when $x = y = z = u$, in which case each term is equal and the arithmetic and geometric means are equal. This gives the maximum value of $C$, which is $C = 16$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$, the following inequality holds:
$$
a^b b^c c^a \leq C a^a b^b c^c.
$$
solution:
I. solution. Since $a, b, c$ are positive numbers, both sides of the inequality are positive. Take the base 10 logarithm of both sides of the inequality. This function is strictly monotonically increasing, so the direction of the relation remains unchanged.

$$
\lg \left(a^{b} b^{c} c^{a}\right) \leq \lg \left(a^{a} b^{b} c^{c}\right)
$$

Now apply the identities for the logarithm of a product and a power.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lg \left(a^{b}\right)+\lg \left(b^{c}\right)+\lg \left(c^{a}\right) & \leq \lg \left(a^{a}\right)+\lg \left(b^{b}\right)+\lg \left(c^{c}\right) \\
b \cdot \lg a+c \cdot \lg b+a \cdot \lg c & \leq a \cdot \lg a+b \cdot \lg b+c \cdot \lg c
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the rearrangement theorem, which states that the sum of products of two sequences of real numbers of the same length is maximized when the sequences are similarly ordered.

Let the two three-element sequences be $a, b, c$ and $\lg a, \lg b, \lg c$. Due to the strictly monotonically increasing nature of the logarithm function, the two sequences are similarly ordered, so

$$
b \cdot \lg a+c \cdot \lg b+a \cdot \lg c \leq a \cdot \lg a+b \cdot \lg b+c \cdot \lg c
$$

holds, and due to the equivalence of the transformations, the original inequality is also true. Equality holds when $a=b=c$.

II. solution. First, we cite a useful algebraic inequality. Let $a, b, c$ be positive numbers, then

$$
(a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}+(c-a)^{2} \geq 0
$$

After expanding and dividing by two, add $3(a b+b c+c a)$ to both sides.

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 a^{2}+2 b^{2}+2 c^{2}-2 a b-2 b c-2 c a & \geq 0 \\
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-a b-b c-c a & \geq 0 \\
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2 a b+2 b c+2 c a & \geq 3 a b+3 b c+3 c a
\end{aligned}
$$

Now divide both sides by the positive $3(a+b+c)$ to get

$$
\frac{a+b+c}{3} \geq \frac{a b+b c+c a}{a+b+c}
$$

Apply the well-known inequality between weighted means in two versions. First, write the inequality between the weighted geometric and harmonic means for the positive numbers $a, b, c$ with weights $a, b, c$:

$$
\left(a^{a} b^{b} c^{c}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b+c}} \geq \frac{a+b+c}{a \cdot \frac{1}{a}+b \cdot \frac{1}{b}+c \cdot \frac{1}{c}}=\frac{a+b+c}{3}
$$

Then use the inequality between the weighted arithmetic and geometric means for the numbers $a, b, c$ with weights $b, c, a$.

$$
\frac{b \cdot a+c \cdot b+a \cdot c}{a+b+c} \geq\left(a^{b} b^{c} c^{a}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b+c}}
$$

Finally, combining (1), (2), and (3), and raising both sides of the inequality to the power of $(a+b+c)$, we get the statement of the problem:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left(a^{a} b^{b} c^{c}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b+c}} \geq \frac{a+b+c}{3} \geq \frac{a b+b c+c a}{a+b+c} \geq\left(a^{b} b^{c} c^{a}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b+c}} \\
a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} \geq a^{b} b^{c} c^{a}
\end{gathered}
$$

Equality in the inequalities above holds if and only if $a = b = c$. In this case, both sides of the original inequality are equal, and the maximal value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = 1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Given a positive function $f(x)$ defined on $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^+$, such that for all $x_1, x_2 \in D$,
\[
f(\sqrt{x_1 x_2}) \leq \sqrt{f(x_1) f(x_2)},
\]
\[
f^2(x_1) + f^2(x_2) \geq 2 f^2\left(\sqrt{\frac{x_1^2 + x_2^2}{2}}\right),
\]
determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all $x_1, x_2 \in D$,
\[
f(x_1) + f(x_2) \geq 2C f\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}\right).
\]
solution:
Prove using the known two inequalities:
$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[f\left(x_{1}\right)+f\left(x_{2}\right)\right]^{2} } & =f^{2}\left(x_{2}\right)+f^{2}\left(x_{2}\right)+2 f\left(x_{1}\right) f\left(x_{2}\right) \\
& \geqslant 2 f^{2}\left(\sqrt{\frac{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}}{2}}\right)+2 f^{2}\left(\sqrt{x_{1} x_{2}}\right) \\
& =2\left[f^{2}\left(\sqrt{\frac{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}}{2}}\right)+f^{2}\left(\sqrt{x_{1} x_{2}}\right)\right] \\
& \geqslant 4 f^{2}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\sqrt{\frac{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}}{2}}\right)^{2}+\left(\sqrt{x_{1} x_{2}}\right)^{2}\right]}\right) \\
& =4 f^{2}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right)^{2}}\right) \\
& =4 f^{2}\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2}\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f\left(x_{1}\right)+f\left(x_{2}\right) \geqslant 2 f\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2}\right)$.

Equality holds when $x_1 = x_2$, since then all intermediate inequalities become equalities and $f(x_1) + f(x_2) = 2 f(x_1) = 2 f\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}\right)$. This gives the minimum value of $C$, so the maximal constant is $C = 1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

Equality is approached in the limit as $n \to \infty$, since the sum $\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n} \frac{1}{k}$ approaches $\ln 2$ and $\ln 2 > \frac{1}{2}$, but for all finite $n$ the sum is always strictly greater than $\frac{1}{2}$. problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all non-negative real numbers $x, y, z$ satisfying $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = x + y + z$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x^{5}+x+1}}+\frac{y+1}{\sqrt{y^{5}+y+1}}+\frac{z+1}{\sqrt{z^{5}+z+1}} \geq C.
$$
solution:
Solution. First we factor $x^{5}+x+1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{5}+x+1 & =x^{5}-x^{2}+x^{2}+x+1=x^{2}\left(x^{3}-1\right)+x^{2}+x+1=x^{2}(x-1)\left(x^{2}+x+1\right)+x^{2}+x+1 \\
& =\left(x^{2}+x+1\right)\left(x^{2}(x-1)+1\right)=\left(x^{2}+x+1\right)\left(x^{3}-x^{2}+1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $A M-G M$ inequality, we have

$$
\sqrt{x^{5}+x+1}=\sqrt{\left(x^{2}+x+1\right)\left(x^{3}-x^{2}+1\right)} \leq \frac{x^{2}+x+1+x^{3}-x^{2}+1}{2}=\frac{x^{3}+x+2}{2}
$$

and since

$x^{3}+x+2=x^{3}+1+x+1=(x+1)\left(x^{2}-x+1\right)+x+1=(x+1)\left(x^{2}-x+1+1\right)=(x+1)\left(x^{2}-x+2\right)$,

then

$$
\sqrt{x^{5}+x+1} \leq \frac{(x+1)\left(x^{2}-x+2\right)}{2}
$$

Using $x^{2}-x+2=\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{7}{4}>0$, we obtain $\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x^{5}+x+1}} \geq \frac{2}{x^{2}-x+2}$ Applying the CauchySchwarz inequality and the given condition, we get

$$
\sum_{c y c} \frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x^{5}+x+1}} \geq \sum_{c y c} \frac{2}{x^{2}-x+2} \geq \frac{18}{\sum_{c y c}\left(x^{2}-x+2\right)}=\frac{18}{6}=3
$$

which is the desired result.

For the equality both conditions: $x^{2}-x+2=y^{2}-y+2=z^{2}-z+2$ (equality in CBS) and $x^{3}-x^{2}+1=x^{2}+x+1$ (equality in AM-GM) have to be satisfied.

By using the given condition it follows that $x^{2}-x+2+y^{2}-y+2+z^{2}-z+2=6$, hence $3\left(x^{2}-x+2\right)=6$, implying $x=0$ or $x=1$. Of these, only $x=0$ satisfies the second condition. We conclude that equality can only hold for $x=y=z=0$.

It is an immediate check that indeed for these values equality holds.

Equality is achieved when $x = y = z = 0$, which satisfies the original constraint and makes the sum equal to $3$. This gives the minimum value of the expression, so the maximal constant $C$ is $3$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 3$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all positive integers $n$ and all sequences $\{a_k\}$ defined by $a_1 = \frac{1}{2}$ and $a_{k+1} = -a_k + \frac{1}{2-a_k}$ for $k \geq 1$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\left[\frac{n}{2(a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n)} - 1\right]^n \leq C \cdot \left(\frac{a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n}{n}\right)^n \cdot \prod_{k=1}^n \left(\frac{1}{a_k} - 1\right).
$$
solution:
Proof. First, prove by mathematical induction: $0 < a_i < \frac{1}{2}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, and the inequality holds for $n$. We need to prove that it also holds for $n+1$.
Thus, the original inequality is equivalent to
$$
\left(\frac{n}{a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}}\right)^{n} \cdot\left(\frac{n}{2\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)}-1\right)^{n} \leqslant\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{a_{2}}-1\right) \cdots\left(\frac{1}{a_{n}}-1\right).
$$

Let $f(x)=\ln \left(\frac{1}{x}-1\right), x \in\left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right)$, then by $f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{-1}{x-x^{2}} < 0$, we know that $f(x)$ is a concave function in $\left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right)$. By Jensen's inequality:
$$
f\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}{n}\right) \leqslant \frac{f\left(x_{1}\right)+f\left(x_{2}\right)+\cdots+f\left(x_{n}\right)}{n}.
$$

Taking $x_{i}=a_{i} (i=1,2, \cdots, n)$, we have
$$
\left(\frac{n}{a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}}-1\right)^{n} \leqslant\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{a_{2}}-1\right) \cdots\left(\frac{1}{a_{n}}-1\right).
$$

On the other hand, by the given condition and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(1-a_{i}\right) & =\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{i}+a_{i+1}}-n \\
& \geqslant \frac{n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(a_{i}+a_{i+1}\right)}-n=\frac{n^{2}}{a_{n+1}-a_{1}+2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}}-n \geqslant \frac{n^{2}}{2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}}-n \\
& =n \cdot\left(\frac{n}{2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}}-1\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(1-a_{i}\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}} \geqslant \frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}}\left(\frac{n}{2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}}-1\right)$.

Therefore,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left(\frac{n}{a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}}\right)^{n} \cdot\left[\frac{n}{2\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)}-1\right]^{n} \leqslant\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(1-a_{i}\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}}\right]^{n} \\
=\left[\frac{\left(1-a_{1}\right)+\left(1-a_{2}\right)+\cdots+\left(1-a_{n}\right)}{a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}}\right]^{n}=\left(\frac{n}{a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}}-1\right)^{n} \\
\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{a}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{a_{2}}-1\right) \cdots\left(\frac{1}{a_{n}}-1\right). \text{ Hence, the proposition is proved. }
\end{array}
$$

Equality holds when all $a_k$ are equal, i.e., $a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_n = \frac{1}{2}$, which is possible only for $n=1$ since $a_1 = \frac{1}{2}$ and the recurrence gives $a_2 = 0$. For $n=1$, the inequality becomes equality, and for $n > 1$, strict inequality holds. Thus, the maximum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = 1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem: Let $\boldsymbol{a}_1, \ldots, \boldsymbol{a}_n$ and $\boldsymbol{b}_1, \ldots, \boldsymbol{b}_m$ be two sets of vectors. Determine the largest constant $C$ such that, if for every line $\ell$, the sum of the lengths of the projections of the $\boldsymbol{a}_i$ onto $\ell$ is at most $C$ times the sum of the lengths of the projections of the $\boldsymbol{b}_j$ onto $\ell$, then necessarily $\sum_{i=1}^n \|\boldsymbol{a}_i\| \leq C \sum_{j=1}^m \|\boldsymbol{b}_j\|$.
solution:

problem:
Determine the minimal constant C such that for all integers n \geq 1, all real numbers p > 1, and all sequences of non-negative real numbers a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n, the following inequality holds:
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} a_{i}}{k}\right)^{p} \leq C \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}^{p}.
\]
solution:
Let $A_{k} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} a_{i}}{k}$. By Hölder's inequality, we have
$$
\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}^{p}\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{k}^{p}\right)^{p-1} \geqslant\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k} A_{k}^{p-1}\right)^{p} \text {. }
$$

It suffices to prove: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k} A_{k}^{p-1} \geqslant \frac{p-1}{p} \sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{k}^{p}$. In fact,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k} A_{k}^{p-1} \\
=a_{1}^{p}+\sum_{k=2}^{n}\left(k A_{k}^{p}-(k-1) A_{k-1} A_{k}^{p}-1\right) \\
=\sum_{k=1}^{n} k A_{k}^{p}-\sum_{k=2}^{n}(k-1) A_{k-1} A_{k}^{p-1} \\
\geqslant \sum_{k=1}^{n} k A_{k}^{p}-\sum_{k=2}^{n} \frac{k-1}{p}\left(A_{k-1}^{p}+(p-1) A_{k}^{p}\right) \\
=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \frac{p-1}{p} A_{k}^{p}+\frac{n+p-1}{p} A_{n} \\
\geqslant \frac{p-1}{p} \sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{k}^{p} .
\end{array}
$$

Equality holds when all $a_k$ are zero except for one $a_j > 0$, i.e., when the sequence is concentrated at a single index. In this case, the ratio $\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n \left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^k a_i}{k}\right)^p}{\sum_{k=1}^n a_k^p}$ achieves its maximum value, which is $\left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p$. Thus, this gives the minimal constant $C$ for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p.$.

problem:

$$
(x-1)(y-1)(z-1) \geq C.
$$
solution:
Solution. From the condition of the problem, it follows that $x y + y z + z x = x y z$. Furthermore, from the condition of the problem and the inequality between the arithmetic and geometric means, we have

$$
x + y + z = (x + y + z)\left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}\right) \geq 3(x y z)^{\frac{1}{3}} \cdot 3\left(\frac{1}{x y z}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = 9
$$

Therefore,

$$
(x-1)(y-1)(z-1) = x y z - x y - y z - z x + x + y + z - 1 \geq 8
$$

Clearly, the equality holds if and only if $x = y = z = 3$. In this case, $(x-1)(y-1)(z-1) = 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$, so the minimum value of $(x-1)(y-1)(z-1)$ is $8$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 8.$.

problem:
Determine the minimal real constant $C$ such that for all events $A$, $B$, $C$ in a probability space, the following inequality holds:
$$
|\mathrm{P}(A \cap B) - \mathrm{P}(A \cap C)| \leq C \cdot \mathrm{P}(B \triangle C).
$$
solution:
Solution. We have

$$
|\mathrm{P}(A B)-\mathrm{P}(A C)| \leqslant \mathrm{P}(A B \triangle A C) \leqslant \mathrm{P}(B \triangle C)
$$

Equality holds when $A$ is a subset of $B \triangle C$, for example when $A = B \setminus C$ or $A = C \setminus B$, in which case $|\mathrm{P}(A \cap B) - \mathrm{P}(A \cap C)| = \mathrm{P}(B \triangle C)$. This gives the maximum value, so the minimal constant $C$ is $1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:

solution:
Analysis We still transform the boundary angle relationship.

So $\frac{a}{1-\sin A}=\frac{2 \sin A}{1-\sin A}=\frac{2 \sin A(1+\sin A)}{(1-\sin A)(1+\sin A)}$
$$
=\frac{2 \sin A+2 \sin ^{2} A}{\cos ^{2} A}=\frac{2 \tan A}{\cos A}+2 \tan ^{2} A
$$

Similarly: $\frac{b}{1-\sin B}=\frac{2 \tan B}{\cos B}+2 \tan ^{2} B, \frac{c}{1-\sin C}=\frac{2 \tan C}{\cos C}+2 \tan ^{2} C$
Also, by $\tan A+\tan B+\tan C=\tan A \tan B \tan C$
It is easy to know: $\tan A \tan B \tan C \geqslant 3 \sqrt{3}$
And $\cos A \cos B \cos C \leqslant \frac{1}{8}$
$$

\tan ^{2} A+\tan ^{2} B+\tan ^{2} C \geqslant 3 \sqrt[3]{(\tan A \tan B \tan C)^{2}}=9 \\
\frac{\tan A}{\cos A}+\frac{\tan B}{\cos B}+\frac{\tan C}{\cos C} \geqslant 3 \sqrt[3]{\frac{\tan A \tan B \tan C}{\cos A \cos B \cos C}} \geqslant 3 \sqrt[3]{\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{\frac{1}{8}}}=6 \sqrt{3}
\end{array}
$$

Therefore, the left side $\geqslant 2(9+6 \sqrt{3})=18+12 \sqrt{3}$, equality holds if and only if $A=B=C=\frac{\pi}{3}$.

Equality is achieved when the triangle is equilateral, i.e., $A = B = C = \frac{\pi}{3}$. In this case, the minimum value of the expression is $C = 18 + 12\sqrt{3}$, so this is the maximal constant for which the inequality always holds.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^+$:
$$
\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + 8bc}} + \frac{b}{\sqrt{b^2 + 8ca}} + \frac{c}{\sqrt{c^2 + 8ab}} \geq C.
$$
solution:
Prove that without loss of generality, $\frac{a}{\sqrt{b^{2}+8 b c}} \geqslant \frac{a^{t}}{a^{t}+b^{t}+c^{t}}$, where $a, b, c$ are any positive real numbers, and $t$ is a to-be-determined exponent.
In particular, when $b=c=1$ and $a$ is any positive real number, the above inequality becomes
$$
\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^{2}+8}} \geqslant \frac{a^{t}}{a^{t}+2}, a \in(0,+\infty) \text {. }
$$

Let $f(x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2}+8}}-\frac{x^{t}}{x^{t}+2}$, then we know that $f(x)$ is continuous and differentiable in $(0,+\infty)$, and satisfies $f(x) \geqslant 0$. Since when $x=1$, the function $f(x)$ attains its minimum value 0, so $x=1$ is an extremum point of the function $f(x)$, i.e., $f^{\prime}(1)=0$.
Since $\left.\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2}+8}}\right) \cdot\right|_{x=1}=\left.\frac{8}{\left(x^{2}+8\right) \sqrt{x^{2}+8}}\right|_{x=1}=\frac{8}{27}$,
$$
\left.\left(\frac{x^{t}}{x^{t}+2}\right)^{\prime}\right|_{x=1}=\left.\frac{2 t \cdot x^{t-1}}{\left(x^{t}+2\right)^{2}}\right|_{x=1}=\frac{2}{9} t
$$

Therefore, $f^{\prime}(1)=\frac{8}{27}-\frac{2}{9} t=0$, thus we find $t=\frac{4}{3}$.
Hence, we have $\frac{a}{\sqrt{b^{2}+8 b c}} \geqslant \frac{a^{\frac{4}{3}}}{a^{\frac{4}{3}}+b^{\frac{4}{3}}+c^{\frac{4}{3}}}$ and similarly for the other two inequalities. Adding these three inequalities together proves the original inequality.

Equality holds when $a = b = c$, for example at $a = b = c = 1$, in which case each term is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1^2 + 8 \cdot 1 \cdot 1}} = \frac{1}{3}$, so the sum is $1$. This gives the minimum value of the sum, so $C = 1$ is the maximal constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1.$.

problem:

\frac{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \cdots + a_n^2}{\min_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} (a_i - a_j)^2} \geq C.

solution:
[Proof] Without loss of generality, let $a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{n}$, then
$$
\left(a_{i}-a_{j}\right)^{2} \geqslant M|i-j|^{2} \text {. }
$$

Let $A=n S-\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)^{2}$, then
$$
A=\sum_{i, j=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}-\sum_{i, j=1}^{n} a_{i} a_{j}=\sum_{i, j=1}^{n} a_{i}\left(a_{i}-a_{j}\right) .
$$

Also, $\quad A=\sum_{i, j=1}^{n} a_{j}^{2}-\sum_{i, j=1}^{n} a_{i} a_{j}=\sum_{i, j=1}^{n} a_{j}\left(a_{j}-a_{i}\right)$,
thus
$$
A=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i, j=1}^{n}\left(a_{i}-a_{j}\right)^{2} .
$$

From (1) and (2), we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
n S & \geqslant A \geqslant \frac{M}{2} \sum_{i, j=1}^{n}(i-j)^{2} \\
& =M\left[n\left(1+2^{2}+\cdots+n^{2}\right)-(1+2+\cdots+n)^{2}\right] .
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formulas
$$
\begin{array}{l}
1+2^{2}+\cdots+n^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6} \\
1+2+\cdots+n=\frac{1}{2} n(n+1)
\end{array}
$$

we can derive
$$
\begin{aligned}
n S & \geqslant\left[\frac{n^{2}(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}-\frac{n^{2}(n+1)^{2}}{4}\right] M \\
& =\frac{1}{12} n^{2}(n+1)(4 n+2-3 n-3) M \\
& =\frac{1}{12} n^{2}\left(n^{2}-1\right) M
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\frac{S}{M} \geqslant \frac{n\left(n^{2}-1\right)}{12}$.

Equality holds when the $a_i$ are equally spaced, i.e., $a_i = d \cdot i + c$ for some constants $d \neq 0$ and $c$, so that all consecutive differences $a_{i+1} - a_i$ are equal and minimal. problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all integers $n \geq 2$ and all real numbers $x_1, ..., x_n \in [1,2]$, the following inequality holds:
$$
|x_1 - x_2| + |x_2 - x_3| + \cdots + |x_n - x_1| \leq C(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n).
$$
solution:
Solution. First method. If $a, b \in [1,2]$, then

$$
|a-b|=\frac{1}{3}(a+b)-\frac{2}{3}(2 \min \{a, b\}-\max \{a, b\}) \leq \frac{1}{3}(a+b)
$$

where the equality holds if and only if $\{a, b\}=\{1,2\}$. From this,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|+\ldots+\left|x_{n}-x_{1}\right| & \leq \frac{1}{3}\left(\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right) \ldots+\left(x_{n}+x_{1}\right)\right) \\
& =\frac{2}{3}\left(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where the equality holds if and only if $n$ is even and the $n$-tuple is equal to $(1,2, \ldots, 1,2)$ or $(2,1, \ldots, 2,1)$.

Second method. First, let's assume that cyclically there are no two consecutive equal terms $x_{i}$. We will say that $x_{i}$ is a local minimum if $x_{i-1}>x_{i}$ and $x_{i}<x_{i+1}$ (cyclically). Clearly, the number of local minima is equal to the number of local maxima, and we denote this number by $k$. Then the left side of the inequality can be written in the form

$$
2\left(\sum_{x_{i} \text { is a local maximum }} x_{i}\right)-2\left(\sum_{x_{i} \text { is a local minimum }} x_{i}\right),
$$

so we need to prove the inequality

$$
\frac{4}{3}\left(\sum_{x_{i} \text { is a local maximum }} x_{i}\right) \leq \frac{8}{3}\left(\sum_{x_{i} \text { is a local minimum }} x_{i}\right)+\frac{2}{3}\left(\sum_{x_{i} \text { is not a local extremum }} x_{i}\right) .
$$

However, the last inequality directly follows from

$$
\frac{4}{3}\left(\sum_{x_{i} \text { is a local maximum }} x_{i}\right) \leq \frac{8 k}{3} \leq \frac{8}{3}\left(\sum_{x_{i} \text { is a local minimum }} x_{i}\right) .
$$

In this case, the equality holds if and only if every $x_{i}$ is a local maximum or a local minimum, the sum of the local minima is $k$ (i.e., every local minimum is equal to 1), and the sum of the local maxima is $2k$ (i.e., every local maximum is equal to 2). In other words, equality holds if and only if $n$ is even and the $n$-tuple is equal to $(1,2, \ldots, 1,2)$ or $(2,1, \ldots, 2,1)$.

In the case where there are equal consecutive terms, we can delete one of them and consider the resulting sequence ($\left.y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n-1}\right)$). In this case, the left side of the corresponding inequality is equal to the left side of the inequality for $x_{i}$, while the right side is strictly smaller. This means that it is sufficient to prove the inequality for the numbers $y_{i}$, $i=1,2, \ldots, n-1$. We repeat this until we obtain a sequence of numbers with no equal consecutive terms, and then we apply the already proven inequality to this case.

Equality in the above arguments holds if and only if $n$ is even and the sequence $(x_1, ..., x_n)$ alternates between $1$ and $2$, i.e., $(1,2,1,2,\ldots)$ or $(2,1,2,1,\ldots)$. In this case, the sum $|x_1-x_2|+\cdots+|x_n-x_1|$ attains its maximum possible value relative to $x_1+\cdots+x_n$, so $C=\frac{2}{3}$ is the maximal constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{2}{3}$.

problem:
Determine the largest real constant $C$ such that for all $a > b > 0$ and $t \in \mathbb{Q}^+$, the following inequality holds:
$$
a^t - b^t \geq C.
$$
solution:
Proof Let $t=\frac{m}{n}$, where $m, n \in \mathbf{N}^{*}$.
Since $a>b>0$, we have $a^{m}>b^{m}>0$,
(Note: This is based on the basic property of inequalities: inequalities with both sides positive can be raised to the same power on both sides)
Therefore, $a^{\frac{m}{n}}>b^{\frac{m}{n}}$,
(Note: This is based on the basic property of inequalities: inequalities with both sides positive can be taken to the same root on both sides)
Therefore, $a^{t}>b^{t}$.
Solution Guide The conclusion of this problem is used to study the monotonicity of power functions and exponential functions in Chapter 4. The two properties used in the process can be referred to in Section 1 of this chapter.

Equality holds in the inequality $a^t - b^t \geq C$ only in the limit as $a \to b^+$, in which case $a^t - b^t \to 0$. Thus, the minimum value of $a^t - b^t$ is $0$, so the largest possible value of $C$ is $0$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 0.$.

problem:
Determine the largest real constant $C$ such that for all $a, b, c > 0$, the following inequality holds:
$$
C(a+b+c) \leq \frac{a^4+b^4+c^4}{abc}.
$$
solution:
Proof 1 Construct the matrix
$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{lll}
a^{2} & b^{2} & c^{2} \\
a & b & c \\
a & b & c
\end{array}\right]_{3 \times 3}, \quad A^{\prime}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
a^{2} & b^{2} & c^{2} \\
b & c & a \\
c & a & b
\end{array}\right]_{3 \times 3}
$$

Then $A$ is a matrix with the same order, by equation (16-2), we have
$$
a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4} \geqslant a^{2} b c+a b^{2} c+a b c^{2}=a b c(a+b+c) .
$$

Thus, $a+b+c \leqslant \frac{a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}}{a b c}$.
Proof 2 Construct the matrix $M=\left[\begin{array}{cccc}a^{4} & a^{4} & b^{4} & c^{4} \\ b^{4} & b^{4} & c^{4} & a^{4} \\ c^{4} & c^{4} & a^{4} & b^{4}\end{array}\right]_{3 \times 4}$
By equation (16-1), we have $\left[\left(a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}\right)^{4}\right]^{\frac{1}{4}} \geqslant a^{2} b c+a b^{2} c+a b c^{2}$.
Thus, $a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4} \geqslant a b c(a+b+c)$, which means $a+b+c \leqslant \frac{a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}}{a b c}$.

Equality holds when $a = b = c$, since then $a^4 + b^4 + c^4 = 3a^4$ and $abc(a+b+c) = a^3 \cdot 3a = 3a^4$, so the inequality becomes $C(3a) \leq \frac{3a^4}{a^3} = 3a$, which is an equality for $C = 1$. This gives the maximum value of $C$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1.$.

problem:
Determine the minimal constant $C$ such that for all $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}^+$ with $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n < 1$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\frac{a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \left[1 - (a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n)\right]}{(a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n)(1 - a_1)(1 - a_2) \cdots (1 - a_n)} \leq C.
$$
solution:
Prove that if $a_{n+1}=1-\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)$, then $a_{n+1}>0$, and the original inequality can be transformed into
$$
n^{n+1} a_{1} a_{2} \cdots a_{n+1} \leqslant\left(1-a_{1}\right)\left(1-a_{2}\right) \cdots\left(1-a_{n}\right)\left(1-a_{n+1}\right) .
$$

For each $i(i=1,2, \cdots, n+1)$, by the $n$-variable arithmetic-geometric mean inequality, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
1-a_{i} & =a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}+\cdots+a_{n+1} \\
& \geqslant n \sqrt[n]{a_{1} a_{2} \cdots a_{i-1} a_{i+1} \cdots a_{n+1}}=n \sqrt[n]{\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n+1} a_{i}}{a_{i}}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the above inequality, we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(1-a_{1}\right)\left(1-a_{2}\right) \cdots\left(1-a_{n}\right)\left(1-a_{n+1}\right) \\
\geqslant & n \cdot \sqrt[n]{\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n+1} a_{i}}{a_{1}}} \cdot n \cdot \sqrt[n]{\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n+1} a_{i}}{a_{2}}} \cdot \cdots \cdot n \sqrt[n]{\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n+1} a_{i}}{a_{n}}} \cdot n \sqrt[n]{\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n+1} a_{i}}{a_{n+1}}}=n^{n+1} a_{1} a_{2} \cdots a_{n+1},
\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that inequality (2) holds, and hence inequality (1) also holds.

Equality in the above inequalities holds when $a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{n+1}$, that is, when all variables are equal and their sum is $1$. In this case, the maximum value of the original expression is achieved, so $C = \frac{1}{n^{n+1}}$ is the minimal constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{1}{n^{n+1}}.$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all $a, b, c, d \in [0,1]$:
$$
(a+b+c+d+1)^2 \geq C(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2).
$$
solution:
We can assume that $a \geq b \geq c \geq d$. Then

$(a+b+c+d+1)^{2}=\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}\right)+2(a b+a c+a d+b c+b d+c d)+2(a+b+c+d)+1 \geq$

$\geq\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}\right)+2\left(b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+d^{2}\right)+2\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}\right)+a^{2} \geq 4\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}\right)$.

Equality holds when $a = b = c = d = 1$, since then $(a+b+c+d+1)^2 = 5^2 = 25$ and $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2 = 4$, so $25 = 4 \times 4 = 16$ only if $C = 4$. This gives the maximum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 4$.

problem:
Determine the minimal constant $C$ such that for all positive integers $n$ and all sequences $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n;\ b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n \in [1,2]$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{a_i^3}{b_i} \leq C \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2.
$$
solution:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\frac{1}{2} \leqslant \frac{a_{i}}{b_{i}} \leqslant 2 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{\frac{a_{i}^{3}}{b_{i}}}}{\sqrt{a_{i} b_{i}}} \leqslant 2 \Rightarrow\left(\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{a_{i} b_{i}}-\sqrt{\frac{a_{i}^{3}}{b_{i}}}\right)\left(2 \sqrt{a_{i} b_{i}}-\sqrt{\frac{a_{i}^{3}}{b_{i}}}\right) \leqslant 0 \\
\Rightarrow a_{i} b_{i}-\frac{5}{2} a_{i}^{2}+\frac{a_{i}^{3}}{b_{i}} \leqslant 0 \Rightarrow \frac{a_{i}^{3}}{b_{i}} \leqslant \frac{5}{2} a_{i}^{2}-a_{i} b_{i}, \\
\frac{1}{2} \leqslant \frac{a_{i}}{b_{i}} \leqslant 2 \Rightarrow\left(\frac{1}{2} b_{i}-a_{i}\right)\left(2 b_{i}-a_{i}\right) \leqslant 0 \Rightarrow a_{i}^{2}+b_{i}^{2}-\frac{5}{2} a_{i} b_{i} \leqslant 0 \\
\Rightarrow-a_{i} b_{i} \leqslant-\frac{2}{5}\left(a_{i}^{2}+b_{i}^{2}\right), \text{ thus } \frac{a_{i}^{3}}{b_{i}} \leqslant \frac{5}{2} a_{i}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}\left(a_{i}^{2}+b_{i}^{2}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Therefore, $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{a_{i}^{3}}{b_{i}} \leqslant \frac{5}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}^{2}\right)=\left(\frac{5}{2}-\frac{4}{5}\right) \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}=\frac{17}{10} \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}$.

Equality holds when $\frac{a_{i}}{b_{i}}=\frac{1}{2}$ or $2$, and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{i}^{2}$, which is achieved when $a_{i}$ is half $1$ and half $2$ (for even $n$), and $a_{i} b_{i}=2$ for all $i$. This gives the maximum value of $C$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{17}{10}.$.

problem:
Determine the maximal real constant C such that for any triangle ABC and any point P inside the triangle, the following inequality holds:
$$
PA + PB + PC \leq C (AB + BC + CA).
$$
solution:
If $M$ is a point inside triangle $A B C$, then $M B+M C<A B+A C$.

Let $M$ be a point inside triangle $A B C$. We need to prove that

$$
M B+M C<A B+A C
$$

To do this, extend $B M$ until it intersects side $A C$ at point $N$ and apply the triangle inequality to triangles $A B N$ and $M N C$.

Similarly, we can prove that

$$
M B+M A<A C+B C \text{ and } M A+M C<A B+B C.
$$

Adding these three inequalities term by term, we get the required inequality.

From this, the required inequality follows.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_08342b966a7aba566077g-02.jpg?height=343&width=644&top_left_y=111&top_left_x=707)

Equality holds when $P$ coincides with one of the triangle's vertices, say $P = A$, in which case $PA + PB + PC = AB + AC = AB + BC + CA - BC$. Since $P$ must be inside the triangle (not on the boundary), strict inequality holds for all interior points, and the maximum value of $C$ is $1$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for any $n \geq 1$ and any $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in I$, the following inequality holds:
$$
f\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right) \leq C \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i).
$$
solution:
【Analysis】First, use mathematical induction to prove: when $n=2^{k}$, the proposition holds.
When $n=2^{k+1}$,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
f\left(\frac{1}{2^{k+1}} \sum_{i=1}^{2^{k+1}} x_{i}\right) \\
=f\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=1}^{2^{k}} x_{i}+\frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=2^{k}+1}^{2^{k+1}} x_{i}\right)\right) \\
\leqslant \frac{1}{2}\left(f\left(\frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=1}^{2^{k}} x_{i}\right)+f\left(\frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=2^{k}+1}^{2^{k+1}} x_{i}\right)\right) \\
\leqslant \frac{1}{2^{k+1}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{2^{k}} f\left(x_{i}\right)+\sum_{i=2^{k}+1}^{2^{k+1}} f\left(x_{i}\right)\right) \\
=\frac{1}{2^{k+1}} \sum_{i=1}^{2^{k+1}} f\left(x_{i}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Then, for any $n \neq 2^{m}$, there exists $k \in \mathbf{Z}_{+}$, $2^{k-1}<n<2^{k}$, in
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\quad f\left(\frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=1}^{2^{k}} x_{i}\right) \leqslant \frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=1}^{2^{k}} f\left(x_{i}\right) \\
\text { let } x_{n+1}=x_{n+2}=\cdots=x_{2^{k}}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} \text {, then } \\
f\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}\right)=f\left(\frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}+\frac{\left(2^{k}-n\right)}{2^{k} n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}\right) \\
=f\left(\frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=1}^{2^{k}} x_{i}\right) \leqslant \frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{i=1}^{2^{k}} f\left(x_{i}\right) \\
=\frac{1}{2^{k}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} f\left(x_{i}\right)+\left(2^{k}-n\right) f\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}\right)\right) \\
\Rightarrow f\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}\right) \leqslant \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f\left(x_{i}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Equality holds when all $x_i$ are equal, i.e., $x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n$, in which case $f\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right) = f(x_1) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i)$. This gives the maximum value of $C$ as $C = \frac{1}{n}$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{1}{n}$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ satisfying $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + (a+b+c)^2 \leq 4$:
$$
\frac{ab+1}{(a+b)^2} + \frac{bc+1}{(b+c)^2} + \frac{ca+1}{(c+a)^2} \geq C.
$$
solution:
The condition becomes $2 \geq a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+a b+b c+c a$. Therefore,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{\text {cyc }} \frac{2 a b+2}{(a+b)^{2}} \geq \sum_{\text {cyc }} \frac{2 a b+\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+a b+b c+c a\right)}{(a+b)^{2}} \\
=\sum_{\text {cyc }} \frac{(a+b)^{2}+(c+a)(c+b)}{(a+b)^{2}} \\
=3+\sum_{\text {сус }} \frac{(c+a)(c+b)}{(a+b)^{2}} \\
\geq 3+3 \sqrt[3]{\prod_{\text {cyc }} \frac{(c+a)(c+b)}{(a+b)^{2}}}=3+3=6 \\
\end{array}
$$
with the last line by AM-GM. This completes the proof.

Equality in the AM-GM step holds when $a = b = c$, and under the constraint $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + (a+b+c)^2 = 4$, this occurs at $a = b = c = 1$. Substituting $a = b = c = 1$ into the original expression gives $\frac{1\cdot1+1}{(1+1)^2} + \frac{1\cdot1+1}{(1+1)^2} + \frac{1\cdot1+1}{(1+1)^2} = 3 \times \frac{2}{4} = 3 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1.5$. However, the solution above shows the minimum value is $C = 3$, so the minimum is achieved at the boundary of the constraint, and $C = 3$ is the maximal constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 3$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all positive real numbers $x, y, z$, the following inequality holds:
$$
(2x+y+z)^2\left(2x^2+(y+z)^2\right) + (2y+z+x)^2\left(2y^2+(z+x)^2\right) + (2z+x+y)^2\left(2z^2+(x+y)^2\right) \leq C.
$$
solution:
## Solution

If the inequality holds for $x, y, z$, then it also holds for $kx, ky, kz$, so it is sufficient to prove the result for $x+y+z=3$. The first term becomes $(x+3)^{2} /\left(2 x^{2}+(3-x)^{2}\right)=(1 / 3)\left(x^{2}+6 x+9\right) /\left(x^{2}-2 x+3\right)=(1 / 3)(1+(8 x+6) /(2+(x-1)^{2})) \leq(1 / 3)(1+(8 x+6) / 2)=4 / 3+4 x / 3$. Similarly for the other terms, so the whole expression $\leq(4 / 3+4 x / 3)+(4 / 3+4 y / 3)+(4 / 3+4 z / 3)=8$.

Equality holds when $x = y = z = 1$, since then each term is maximized and the sum equals $8$. Thus, this gives the maximum value of $C$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 8.$.

problem:
Determine the largest real constant $C$ such that for all $(X_1, X_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, the inequality
$$
P(X_1, X_2) = X_1^2 + (1 - X_1 X_2)^2 \geq C
$$
holds.
solution:
First, $P\left(X_{1}, X_{2}\right)$ is a sum of two squares, so inf $P\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right) \geq$ 0. On the other hand, if $\varepsilon>0$ is an arbitrarily small real number, then $P\left(\varepsilon^{1 / 2}, \varepsilon^{-1 / 2}\right)=\varepsilon$, so that $\inf P\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)$.

Therefore, if $P$ attains its minimum at a point $(x, y)$, then we have $0=\partial_{x_{1}} P(x, y)=$ $\partial_{x_{2}} P(x, y)$, that is, $0=2 x-2 y(1-x y)=-2 x(1-x y)$. In particular, if $1-x y=0$, we deduce that $x=0$, which is absurd. This is why $1-x y \neq 0$, so $x=0$ and $y=0$. However, $P(0,0)=1>0=\inf P\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)$. Therefore, $P$ does not admit a minimum.

Equality is approached (but never attained) as $X_1 \to 0$ and $X_2 \to \infty$ in such a way that $X_1^2 \to 0$ and $1 - X_1 X_2 \to 0$, for example, by taking $X_1 = \varepsilon^{1/2}$ and $X_2 = \varepsilon^{-1/2}$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$. Thus, the minimum value of $C$ is $0$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 0$.

problem:
Determine the largest real constant $C$ such that for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a^3 + b^3 = 1$, the following inequality holds:
$$
a^2 + ab + b^2 - a - b \geq C.
$$
solution:
I. solution. If $a^{3}+b^{3}=1$ and $a, b$ are positive numbers, then $a, b < 1$ \\
a^{2}+b^{2}+(a-1)(b-1)-a^{3}-b^{3} & >0 \\
a^{2}(1-a)+b^{2}(1-b)+(a-1)(b-1) & >0
\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $0 < a, b < 1$, so $a > a^{2} > a^{3}$ and $b > b^{2} > b^{3}$. Multiply the inequality by 2 and show from the left side that it is positive. In the process, we will use the condition again.

$$
\begin{gathered}
2 a^{2}+2 a b+2 b^{2}-2 a-2 b>a^{2}+a^{3}+2 a b+b^{2}+b^{3}-2 a-2 b= \\
=a^{2}+b^{2}+2 a b-2 a-2 b+1=(a+b-1)^{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

We know that $a+b > a^{3}+b^{3}=1$, so $(a+b-1)^{2}>0$.

Equality holds when $a^3 + b^3 = 1$ and $a + b = 1$, which occurs when $a = 1$, $b = 0$ or $a = 0$, $b = 1$, but since $a, b > 0$, the minimum is approached as $a \to 1$, $b \to 0^+$ (or vice versa), and in this case $a^2 + ab + b^2 - a - b \to 0$. Thus, the minimum value of the expression is $C = 0$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 0$.

problem:
Determine the largest real constant $C$ such that for any sequence of real numbers $a_1, a_2, ..., a_n$ and any non-decreasing sequence $x_1 \leq x_2 \leq ... \leq x_n$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\max\{|x_i - a_i| : 1 \leq i \leq n\} \geq C \cdot d,
$$
where $d = \max\{\max\{a_j : 1 \leq j \leq i\} - \min\{a_j : i \leq j \leq n\} : 1 \leq i \leq n\}$.
solution:
Solution 1. (a) Let $1 \leq p \leq q \leq r \leq n$ be indices for which
$$
d=d_{q}, \quad a_{p}=\max \left\{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq q\right\}, \quad a_{r}=\min \left\{a_{j}: q \leq j \leq n\right\}
$$
and thus $d=a_{p}-a_{r}$. (These indices are not necessarily unique.)
For arbitrary real numbers $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$, consider just the two quantities $\left|x_{p}-a_{p}\right|$ and $\left|x_{r}-a_{r}\right|$. Since
$$
\left(a_{p}-x_{p}\right)+\left(x_{r}-a_{r}\right)=\left(a_{p}-a_{r}\right)+\left(x_{r}-x_{p}\right) \geq a_{p}-a_{r}=d,
$$
we have either $a_{p}-x_{p} \geq \frac{d}{2}$ or $x_{r}-a_{r} \geq \frac{d}{2}$. Hence,
$$
\max \left\{\left|x_{i}-a_{i}\right|: 1 \leq i \leq n\right\} \geq \max \left\{\left|x_{p}-a_{p}\right|,\left|x_{r}-a_{r}\right|\right\} \geq \max \left\{a_{p}-x_{p}, x_{r}-a_{r}\right\} \geq \frac{d}{2} \text {. }
$$
(b) Define the sequence $\left(x_{k}\right)$ as
$$
x_{1}=a_{1}-\frac{d}{2}, \quad x_{k}=\max \left\{x_{k-1}, a_{k}-\frac{d}{2}\right\} \quad \text { for } 2 \leq k \leq n .
$$

We show that we have equality in (1) for this sequence.
By the definition, sequence $\left(x_{k}\right)$ is non-decreasing and $x_{k}-a_{k} \geq-\frac{d}{2}$ for all $1 \leq k \leq n$. Next we prove that
$$
x_{k}-a_{k} \leq \frac{d}{2} \quad \text { for all } 1 \leq k \leq n .
$$

Consider an arbitrary index $1 \leq k \leq n$. Let $\ell \leq k$ be the smallest index such that $x_{k}=x_{\ell}$. We have either $\ell=1$, or $\ell \geq 2$ and $x_{\ell}>x_{\ell-1}$. In both cases,
$$
x_{k}=x_{\ell}=a_{\ell}-\frac{d}{2} .
$$

Since
$$
a_{\ell}-a_{k} \leq \max \left\{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq k\right\}-\min \left\{a_{j}: k \leq j \leq n\right\}=d_{k} \leq d,
$$
equality (3) implies
$$

problem:

solution:
Prove that since $\frac{1}{k(n+1-k)}=\frac{1}{n+1}\left(\frac{1}{k}+\frac{1}{n+1-k}\right)$, therefore $a_{n}=\frac{2}{n+1} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k}$,
Thus, for any positive integer $n \geqslant 2$, we have
$$

i.e., $a_{n+1}<a_{n}$.

problem: Determine the largest real constant $C$ such that for all positive integers $n$, if $x_n$ is the unique positive real solution to $x_n^n = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_n^j$, then $x_n < C$.

and

g_{n}\left(2-\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right)=-\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\left(2-\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right)^{n}+1=1-2\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right)^{n}<0,

Equality $x_n = C$ is approached in the limit as $n \to \infty$, since $x_n \to 2$ from below, but for all finite $n$, $x_n < 2$. Thus, the maximum value of $C$ for which $x_n < C$ for all $n$ is $C = 2$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all integers $n \geq 1$ and all sequences of real numbers $a_0, a_1, ..., a_n$ with $a_0 = 0$ and $a_{k+1} \geq a_k + 1$ for $k = 0, 1, ..., n-1$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\sum_{k=1}^n a_k^3 \geq C \left(\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\right)^2.
$$
solution:
We will prove the statement by induction. The base case ($n=1$) is obvious.

Induction step. According to the induction hypothesis, $\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n+1} a_{k}\right)^{2}=a_{n+1}^{2}+2 a_{n+1} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}+\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}\right)^{2} \leq$ $a_{n+1}^{2}+2 a_{n+1} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}+\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}^{3}$

Thus, it is sufficient to check that $a_{n+1}^{3} \geq a_{n+1}^{2}+2 a_{n+1} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}$, or that

$a_{n+1}^{2}-a_{n+1} \geq 2 \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}$

To prove the latter statement, note that

$a_{k+1}+a_{k} \leq\left(a_{k+1}+a_{k}\right)\left(a_{k+1}-a_{k}\right)=a_{k+1}^{2}-a_{k}^{2}$.

Summing the obtained inequalities over $k$ from 0 to $n$, we arrive at the inequality

$a_{n+1}+2 \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k} \leq \sum_{k=0}^{n}\left(a_{k+1}^{2}-a_{k}^{2}\right)=a_{n+1}^{2}, \quad$ as required.

Equality holds when the sequence increases by exactly $1$ at each step, i.e., $a_k = k$ for $k = 0, 1, ..., n$. In this case, $\sum_{k=1}^n a_k^3 = \left(\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\right)^2$, so $C = 1$ is the maximal constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 1$.

problem:
Determine the maximal real constant $C$ such that for all integers $n \geq 2$ and all real sequences $x_1 \geq x_2 \geq \cdots \geq x_n$ and $y_1 \geq y_2 \geq \cdots \geq y_n$ satisfying
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i = 0, \quad \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2 = 1,

the following inequality holds:
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i y_i - x_i y_{n+1-i}) \geq C.
$$
solution:
We present two approaches. In both approaches, it's helpful motivation that for even $n$, equality occurs at
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left(x_{i}\right)=(\underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}, \ldots, \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}}_{n / 2}, \underbrace{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}, \ldots,-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}}_{n / 2}) \\
\left(y_{i}\right)=(\frac{n-1}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}},-\underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}, \ldots,-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}}_{n-1})
\end{array}
$$

『 First approach (expected value). For a permutation $\sigma$ on $\{1,2, \ldots, n\}$ we define
$$
S_{\sigma}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} y_{\sigma(i)}
$$

Claim - For random permutations $\sigma, \mathbb{E}\left[S_{\sigma}\right]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}\left[S_{\sigma}^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{n-1}$.
Proof. The first one is clear.
Since $\sum_{i<j} 2 x_{i} x_{j}=-1$, it follows that (for fixed $i$ and $j$ ), $\mathbb{E}\left[y_{\sigma(i)} y_{\sigma(j)}\right]=-\frac{1}{n(n-1)}$, Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2} \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[y_{\sigma(i)}^{2}\right] & =\frac{1}{n} \\
2 \sum_{i<j} x_{i} x_{j} \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[y_{\sigma(i)} y_{\sigma(j)}\right] & =(-1) \cdot \frac{1}{n(n-1)}
\end{aligned}
$$
the conclusion follows.
Claim (A random variable in $[0,1]$ has variance at most $1 / 4)$ - If $A$ is a random
variable with mean $\mu$ taking values in the closed interval $[m, M]$ then
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(A-\mu)^{2}\right] \leq \frac{1}{4}(M-m)^{2} .
$$

Proof. By shifting and scaling, we may assume $m=0$ and $M=1$, so $A \in[0,1]$ and hence $A^{2} \leq A$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(A-\mu)^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[A^{2}\right]-\mu^{2} \leq \mathbb{E}[A]-\mu^{2}=\mu-\mu^{2} \leq \frac{1}{4} .
$$

This concludes the proof.
Thus the previous two claims together give
$$
\max _{\sigma} S_{\sigma}-\min _{\sigma} S_{\sigma} \geq \sqrt{\frac{4}{n-1}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}} .
$$

But $\sum_{i} x_{i} y_{i}=\max _{\sigma} S_{\sigma}$ and $\sum_{i} x_{i} y_{n+1-i}=\min _{\sigma} S_{\sigma}$ by rearrangement inequality and therefore we are done.

बा Outline of second approach (by convexity, due to Alex Zhai). We will instead prove a converse result: given the hypotheses
- $x_{1} \geq \cdots \geq x_{n}$
- $y_{1} \geq \cdots \geq y_{n}$
- $\sum_{i} x_{i}=\sum_{i} y_{i}=0$
- $\sum_{i} x_{i} y_{i}-\sum_{i} x_{i} y_{n+1-i}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}}$
we will prove that $\sum x_{i}^{2} \sum y_{i}^{2} \leq 1$.
Fix the choice of $y$ 's. We see that we are trying to maximize a convex function in $n$ variables $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ over a convex domain (actually the intersection of two planes with several half planes). So a maximum can only happen at the boundaries: when at most two of the $x$ 's are different.

An analogous argument applies to $y$. In this way we find that it suffices to consider situations where $x_{\bullet}$ takes on at most two different values. The same argument applies to y.
At this point the problem can be checked directly.

Equality in the inequality $\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i y_i - x_i y_{n+1-i}) \geq C$ is achieved when the sequences $x_i$ and $y_i$ are as given in the initial motivation, i.e., $x_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ for $i \leq n/2$, $x_i = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ for $i > n/2$, and $y_1 = \frac{n-1}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}$, $y_2 = \cdots = y_n = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}$. In this case, the minimum value of $\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i y_i - x_i y_{n+1-i})$ is $C = \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}}$, so this is the minimal value of the expression for all such sequences.

Therefore, the answer is $C = \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}}.$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that for all real numbers $a, b, c > 0$ that are the side lengths of a triangle, the following inequality holds:
$$
a^4 + b^4 + c^4 < C(a^2b^2 + a^2c^2 + b^2c^2).
$$
solution:
From the premise, it follows that $a>0 ; b>0 ; c>0$ and $a+b>c ; a+c>b ; b+c>a$.

Thus, it is also true that $a+b+c>0 ; a+b-c>0 ; a-b+c>0 ;-a+b+c>0$.

Multiplying all the last four inequalities together, the claim follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}
(a+b+c)(a+b-c)(a-b+c)(-a+b+c)=-a^{4}-b^{4}-c^{4}+2\left(a^{2} b^{2}+a^{2} c^{2}+b^{2} c^{2}\right)>0 \quad \text { therefore } \\
a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}<2\left(a^{2} b^{2}+a^{2} c^{2}+b^{2} c^{2}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

Equality holds when the triangle is degenerate, i.e., when $a + b = c$, $a + c = b$, or $b + c = a$, but since $a, b, c > 0$ and strict triangle inequalities are required, equality is never achieved for positive side lengths. Thus, $C = 2$ is the maximal constant for which the inequality always holds.

Therefore, the answer is $C = 2$.

problem:
Determine the maximal constant $C$ such that the following inequality holds for all positive real numbers $a_2, ..., a_n$ with $a_2 a_3 \cdots a_n = 1$:
$$
(1+a_2)^2 (1+a_3)^3 \cdots (1+a_n)^n \geq C.
$$
solution:
It is a matter of judiciously cutting each parenthesis to apply the AM-GM inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(1+a_{2}\right)^{2} & \geqslant 2^{2} \times a_{2} \\
\left(1+a_{3}\right)^{3}=\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+a_{3}\right)^{3} & \geqslant 3^{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times a_{3} \\
\left(1+a_{4}\right)^{4}=\left(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+a_{4}\right)^{4} & \geqslant 4^{4} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times a_{4} \\
& \cdots \\
\left(1+a_{n}\right)^{n}=\left(\frac{1}{n-1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n-1}+a_{n}\right)^{n} & \geqslant n^{n} \times \frac{1}{(n-1)^{n-1}} \times a_{n}
\end{aligned}
$$

It only remains to take the product of these inequalities for the exercise to be completed.

Equality in each application of the AM-GM inequality holds when $a_2 = a_3 = \cdots = a_n = 1$. In this case, $a_2 a_3 \cdots a_n = 1$ and $(1+1)^2 (1+1)^3 \cdots (1+1)^n = 2^{2+3+\cdots+n} = n^n$. Thus, the maximum value of $C$ for which the inequality always holds is $C = n^n$.

Therefore, the answer is $C = n^n.$.
